Most commonsense reasoning tasks utilize ATOMIC and ATOMIC-2020 as primary training data. These resources have become de facto standards in the field. Nevertheless, these resources are limited in scope, only encompassing social knowledge, and do not accurately represent the full range of human knowledge. To address this issue, this paper introduces CoSCoRA, a comprehensive set of knowledge-based commonsense reasoning tasks. These tasks are initially trained on a new, diverse knowledge graph called CoSCoRA-KG, which includes a wide array of knowledge types, including physical knowledge. To validate the effectiveness of this new knowledge graph, the paper proposes five novel reasoning tasks built upon CoSCoRA-KG. To showcase the distinctiveness of these tasks, state-of-the-art models developed specifically for existing knowledge graphs, namely ATOMIC and Wikipedia, are adapted to perform on CoSCoRA tasks, which reveals their complete data collapse. To counter this problem, a new approach called Knowledge Graph Adaptation is proposed, outperforming ATOMIC on 4 out of 5 introduced tasks.

This article details the data processing steps taken within the Hi-GAL survey's data pipeline, showcasing its ability to process up to 50 GB of data per day. Incorporating three key techniques - primary beam deaperturing, primary beam weighting, and deconvolution, along with re-synthesis, the pipeline yields approximately 100-200 spatial channels per beam full-width half-maximum per source. Building on existing tools from the PySMIRTEL library, our code is a direct extension of the Hi-GAL team's initial data processing methodology. A comprehensive evaluation of the pipeline's performance is presented through its sensitivity to signal and noise, validated against existing data sets. The processing time for one source per day is estimated at around 10-15 CPU hours using 16 cores, ultimately yielding a final data cube with approximately 15-20 times the original primary beam resolution.

The differences in chemical makeup among the same galaxy's star clusters are a key area of research. To better understand these variations, a study of the chemical abundance of iron and calcium in the very old stars of the NGC 1466 globular cluster has been conducted. The results from the analysis of the stars' chemical makeup have revealed that the cluster contains multiple generations of stars. The variation in the iron content of the multi-generational stars can be explained by the explosion of supernovae of a certain type. The variation in the calcium content of these stars can be attributed to the explosion of supernovae of a different type of star. The age of the first generation of the cluster's stars is estimated to be around 12.8 billion years. The density of the first generation of the cluster's stars is estimated to be around 3 x 10^-3 solar masses per cubic parsec. The mass of the first generation of the cluster's stars is estimated to be around 0.33 solar masses per cubic parsec. The study has also revealed the presence of newly discovered stars in the cluster. The study has revealed that the first generation of the cluster's stars was formed from gas that was largely unaffected by previous supernovae explosions. The second generation of the cluster's stars was formed from gas that was altered by a previous supernovae explosion of a certain type. The findings of the study reveal that the cluster's stars were formed from gas

In one-dimensional systems with two types of particles, a and b, moving along a line, the means square displacement of particle a is used to measure the speed-accuracy trade-off. It has been observed that the displacement trade-off is independent of initial positions and depends on interaction strength and particle density. Notably, the trade-off is particularly sensitive to how particle b influences particle a, and this effect is seen in the diffusive constant of particle a and its variance. These findings are demonstrated with examples from the ABO model, and the data suggests that the trade-off is applicable in the ABO, ABC, and the ABCO dense models.

The speaker introduces an information-theoretic generalization of Bayesian inference under quantum mechanics, denoted as quantum Bayes' rule. This concept is used to reinterpret Frauchiger-Renner's and Hardy's paradoxes, which suggest that no consistent agent quantum theory can exist. Frauchiger-Renner's setup violates the no-superdeterminism principle, while Hardy's setup violates the principle of local causality. Quantum Bayes' rule, however, accommodates all of them without conflict.

The effects of different boundary conditions on quantum field theories can be measured precisely in the context of massless free scalar field theory in three-dimensional space. These field theory calculations, based on Wilson loop nonlocal operators, reveal the power of periodic conditions compared to those of Dirichlet conditions. The differences between these calculations can be calculated exactly and correspond to specific values known as Riemann zeta function values.

Using a novel algebraic transfer, specifically $E_5$, which we define in this paper, any detected non-trivial element is also detected by it. Our research reveals that certain non-trivial elements, such as $h_{10}^2h_2h_3h_7h_9$, cannot be detected by lower transfers, $t_4$ through $t_9$, but are detected by the fifth transfer, $E_5$, which computationally demonstrates $4$-periodic elements beginning at powers of $2$. Our research further shows that $E_5$ leads to several periodicity phenomena.

To assess molecular hydrogen's capacity to filter out Lyman-$\alpha$ photons, 
we take spectral measurements of this gas while it is exposed to radiation of the 
same wavelength within a confined space similar to that present in the 
absorption cell system. A $10 \times 10 \times 10$ cm$^3$ absorption cell, 
containing $200$ Torr of molecular hydrogen, is used to record a high-resolution 
spectrum of the radiation. By comparing this data to a standard reference, 
we are able to quantify how much a specific spectral profile within the 
Rayleigh-Jeans region is reduced due to the presence of molecular hydrogen. 
These measurements are then used to calculate the level of background light that 
can be expected in different parts of the sky as seen by the LiteBIRD telescope, 
taking into account its specific design, including its 27 types of detectors and 
aperture shapes.

This research introduces an adaptive communication strategy for a network of vehicles, each governed by a basic model. The researchers investigate the trade-off between communication costs and vehicle performance in the context of distributed control and communication strategies. They develop an asynchronous communication strategy where vehicles only transmit their updated information when the associated communication costs are justified. This cost measurement reflects the relevant time frame within the communication interval. Theoretical analysis confirms the effectiveness of this cost measurement in achieving a stable and efficient vehicle platoon. The findings also reveal the relationship between communication frequency, communication costs, and vehicle spacing errors. Furthermore, the research extends its concepts to a more complex vehicle model, specifically the nonlinear longitudinal dynamics model.

Advanced image search and copy detection systems rely on a feature extraction technique called hashing, which extracts compact binary representations of images.  When calculating a similarity measure between two images, the Hamming distance is used, and the images are considered similar or dissimilar based on a predetermined threshold.  Although hash functions reduce the likelihood of false positives, they inevitably introduce some false positives, and the goal of hash function design is to minimize them.  In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach called active indexing, which further reduces the likelihood of false positives.  Active indexing applies a separate hashing method to query and database images to recalculate their similarities and presents a novel concept of active vs. passive indexing, where the former actively verifies potential false positives while the latter accepts them.  Our experiments on large-scale visual search and copy detection tasks demonstrate that active indexing outperforms traditional hashing methods in terms of performance and are more effective than existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We explore a method to convert an existing channel code, operating at a rate close to zero, into an authenticated code, without the need for a completely new design. By introducing a non-negligible overhead, we ensure that existing source codes can be integrated with existing channel codes, resulting in a code that approaches a zero error rate. This approach draws on ideas from the Reed-Muller authentication scheme, but our work presents two key improvements: we eliminate the requirement for an infinite block length and we lower the error rate by several orders of magnitude. We demonstrate that this authentication scheme can be applied to any channel code, making it a versatile solution.

This study examines the exceptional superdiffusion phenomenon in systems of Brownian particles within the context of a highly anisotropic environment influenced by two competing forces - a periodic potential and an external linear force - competing for control. To better understand this phenomenon, the research implements an advanced simulation technique, the path integral Monte Carlo method, to analyze the diffusion behavior across various parameter combinations. The simulation data is analyzed using two key metrics, the diffusion exponent and the mean squared displacement, to characterize the diffusion pattern. The simulation reveals that under certain parameter settings, the Brownian diffusion exhibits an unusual superdiffusion behavior with an exponent of 2.5 and an infinite mean squared displacement. The exceptional superdiffusion is also found to be linked to the characteristics of the system's phase space structure. The exceptional superdiffusion is hypothesized to be due to the presence of chaotic saddles that act as an obstacle to the Brownian diffusion, significantly restricting the diffusion behavior.

A new method has been created to assess the economic impact of financial disruptions by combining advanced economic models with techniques that analyze financial market data. To this end, the model utilizes complex networks, identifying the most significant financial shocks based on their real-world occurrence frequency and extreme impact levels. When applied to the US economy, our findings reveal that minor disruptions have primarily local effects, causing minimal overall damage. Conversely, major disruptions have the potential to cause widespread harm. Interestingly, while some disruptions undermine the model's protective mechanisms and increase vulnerability to further damage, others strengthen it. Furthermore, our study sheds light on the impact of large financial transfers to non-financial sectors and how these effects alter with changes in interest rates.

The quantum friction experienced by objects moving through the quantum vacuum is analyzed in relation to the objects' kinetic angular momentum. It's found that as recoil emission increases due to objects moving at different velocities, it exhibits an inverse relationship with angular momentum. This results in objects with higher angular momentum becoming stable, while those with lower angular momentum experiencing stabilization due to quantum effects. These findings suggest that certain patterns in the objects' behavior can be used to accurately calculate the coefficients of quantum friction.

The task of entity typing in narrative texts is a particularly challenging task, largely due to the need for text analysts to assign accurate categories to each mention, despite text analysts' knowledge levels varying widely. To improve this process, we propose the FGNET-RH framework, which incorporates a reactive hypernetwork to dynamically refine category assignments for each mention in a particular text. We test this approach on the FGNET corpus and develop a new, challenging subtask called Mention Reactive Hypernetwork for Entity Typing (MRH-ET). We then introduce a specific model for this subtask that combines the strengths of a standard network and a specialized transformer model.

Functions $g(z)$ analytic in the unit disk are investigated, where $g(z)$ is $\beta$-univalent if and only if $|\arg g(z)|<\pi/2$ for all $g(z)$ and $|z|<1$. For a given function $G(z)$ in the class of starlike functions, a subordination relationship is considered between $g(z)$ and $z+g(z)$, i.e., $g(z)+g'(z)\ll G(z)$. This relationship is further specified by introducing functions $A(z)$ and $B(z)$ that define a new class of functions $S(A,B)$. These are functions $g(z)$ for which $|\arg g(z)|<\pi/2$ for all $g(z)$ and $|z|<1$ with $g(0)=0$ and $g'(0)=1$ and which satisfy $A(z)\ll g(z)+g'(z)$. This relationship is further specified by introducing functions $h(z)$ that are convex in the unit disk, i.e., $h \in C$, and which satisfy $h(0)=0$ and $h'(1)=1$. This class of functions $S(A,B)$ is used to establish bounds for the real part of $g(z)$, i.e., $\Re g(z)$. This bound is in turn used to establish bounds for the real part of $g'(

We propose an innovative Prepartition approach that restructures how virtual machines (VMs) are scheduled, resulting in a significant improvement in how computing resources are utilized. The traditional scheduling method, which utilizes bin-packing, allocates resources to VMs in small increments, leading to inefficient use of unused resources for each scheduled VM. In contrast, Preposition combines the unused resources of multiple VMs prior to scheduling, then distributes them among scheduled VMs, thereby reducing wastage and enhancing overall efficiency. The effectiveness of Prepartition is demonstrated in various simulated scenarios with 1000 VMs, 100 hosts, and 1000 hosts, yielding a 10-15% average increase in resource packing efficiency. The approach is further validated by its successful integration into a production system, yielding a 10-15% average increase in resource packing efficiency in production.

In various two-player games, key equilibrium concepts like ex-post Nash equilibria contain valuable information, making them highly relevant in both theoretical and applied AI research.  To address this, our work focuses on developing a learning approach to predict ex-post Nash equilibria in complex, continuous games where each player has multiple action variables and unlimited utility options.  To this end, a new class of networks called a Nash Fixed Point Network is proposed as a more reliable alternative to a previous approach known as the M-PFP.  This new network has a few notable advantages, including the ability to produce fewer prediction errors, fewer crashes, and fewer rejections of valid test cases.  Our results show that N-FPN is a successful tool for predicting ex-post Nash equilibria in complex games with 2, 3, and 4 variables, outperforming M-PFP in all prediction tasks.  Our research also reveals that both approaches struggle in very complex games, but N-FPN shows more promise for future improvements.

This research introduces a framework for reducing the dimensionality of covariates using pre-study information. By examining the effect of pre-experiment variable selection on bias and estimation precision, we establish a novel method for obtaining a balanced treatment effect estimator. Our estimator utilizes post-experiment variable selection, choosing only variables that significantly impact the outcome. By demonstrating that even small reductions in dimensionality result in a substantial increase in estimation precision, we show the practical value of our approach. Additionally, we provide a new estimator that uses pre-experiment information to select variables, achieving superior performance. Our findings are verified by a simulated and real-world dataset from the National Longitudinal Surveys.

This paper explores the problem of identifying stealthy online attacks in dynamic systems. Building on conventional model predictive control methods, the conventional approach controls an unmonitored attack while detection systems monitor for inconsistencies. Our proposed method, however, incorporates both the attacker and controller into a unified control framework, effectively creating a control system that remains undetected by conventional monitoring systems. To create a more challenging scenario, an online monitoring system tracks the unaltered controller and the reactive system it typically controls for comparison. Our simulation results demonstrate that, on average, the unified monitoring system fails to detect the proposed approach, creating a truly undetectable attack.

A key challenge in document summarization lies in accurately capturing semantic relationships within a document to generate a concise summary. To address this problem, researchers introduced the GAE-ISumm model, which leverages the Graph AutoEncoder (GAE) to incorporate sentence co-occurrence information in enhancing summarization quality. In summarization tasks, the model uses a Single Layer Attention mechanism to train the encoder and encoder reader while employing the entire GAE as the reader in the GAE-ISumm model. Experimental results on two datasets, the New York Times General Summery and the DUTY dataset, demonstrate that the proposed model attains state-of-the-art performance in the DUTY dataset and significantly outperforms the GAE-ISumm model in the GNTT-Summ dataset. Furthermore, the study reveals that incorporating the graph structure in the GAE-ISumm model yields better performance.

For an algebras A, an A-modulation G, and sets S, of algebras of Krull type, which are independent, we show that G/Spec0, the quotient category, and injective dimension, depend on the modules over S and their zero modules S0.

We are currently on the verge of a revolution in the study of planetary systems. This is largely driven by the capabilities of future space-based observatories such as the Extremes and Hyperspace missions. A pivotal element of these missions involves the use of advanced instruments like MICADO, designed to be installed on large telescopes such as the ELT. To further enhance our understanding of these systems, it is essential that we be able to detect and characterize exoplanetary systems with multiple transiting planets. This requires the development of cutting-edge exoplanet models that can be integrated with space-based observatory data. This paper introduces a novel statistical approach to the characterization of multiple transiting planets and assesses its potential by analyzing data from a suite of simulated datasets. The simulations are based on current and future planetary systems, including those discovered by the Kepler and CHEOPS missions, as well as systems that Hubble and MICADO could detect with the assistance of future missions like Extremes and CHEOPS. This study demonstrates that by applying this statistical approach to data collected from the mentioned missions, it is possible to accurately reconstruct the characteristics of exoplanetary systems, including information about the size, orbital patterns, and tidal interactions of individual planets. This is particularly true even for complex multi-planet systems, where it is feasible to detect subtle tidal interactions between planets and to accurately measure the size of individual planets with high levels of precision. This study also provides valuable insights into the future of exoplanet research

We examine the underlying reasons for the typical training procedure of Variational Autoencoders using our created theoretical models. Our findings show that this process achieves a delicate balance between accurately reconstructing input data and appropriately modeling uncertainty. Additionally, our analysis provides insight into the reconstruction accuracy achieved and offers an explanation for a common phenomenon in VAE training where a trade-off occurs between model complexity and uncertainty. We also clarify and correct certain representation theorems for both the encoder and variational decoder of the VAE. These theoretsical insights into VAEs may facilitate a deeper understanding of the behavior of generative neural networks more broadly.

A novel method for locating and monitoring devices in smart home systems utilizes a non-invasive approach, relying on the location information of access points to calculate device positions without requiring direct line-of-sight or visual tracking. By estimating device positions through RSSI-based calculations, a two-stage process involving data filtering and outlier removal refines localization results. These positions are then employed to identify human activities, which are recorded as activity histories over defined timeframes. By combining these histories, individual device associations are constructed, allowing for the inference of device ownership. Experimental findings indicate that this method effectively generates device ownership profiles, comparable in accuracy to methods based on manual input, with ownership identification accuracy of 85.7% and 88.6% for two and three-floor homes, respectively. Furthermore, our findings suggest that this positioning system can achieve localization accuracy within 3 meters.

We introduce an efficient quantization method for learning self-supervised features 
within a large-scale framework. This method makes possible training high-performance 
quantization-based self-supervised methods using hundreds of GPU nodes, utilizing a novel 
partitioning strategy that enables cross-node cross-particle gradient computations. 
Through thorough experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed 
quantization technique over state-of-the-art maximum mutual information quantization 
approaches, all trained using the same number of GPU nodes, and effectively reduce the 
training cost by a significant 1000 times.

This research focuses on optimizing a specific property in directed acyclic graphs based on their given width, by applying a width-based parameter. We explore the underlying connection between parameterized algorithms and the graph's underlying structure, which we term the treewidth. We start by establishing an efficient kernel for the k Shortest Paths problem, which we then use to solve another k-related problem, k Longest Paths, on treewidth-based graphs. We also establish a specific lower bound on the computational requirements for both k-shortest paths and k-longest paths, which we achieve by using a specific width-based graph model. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on other k-related problems, including k-Reachable Vertices and k-Many-Shortest-Paths.

Deep neural networks frequently struggle to provide a balance between accurate labeling and generalization, especially in scenarios with uncertain labeling. In contrast, a classification method that leverages ensemble modeling can effectively handle such uncertainty without compromising performance. By combining the outputs of multiple neural networks, an ensemble model can detect and account for mislabeling, ultimately improving classification and regression tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the robustness of this approach across various datasets.

We establish a concrete criterion for the quasicompactness of transfer operators for both uniformly and nonuniformly expanding semiflows, resulting in a precise rate of asymptotic correlation decay. This criterion depends solely on the size of the perturbations of unstable norms within the phase space, providing an explicit bound. Our method leverages a size-reducing version of Pesin's bundle theorem, allowing the transfer operator to act on a size-reduced family of unstable bundles, thus significantly decreasing the size of transfer operators as it evolves over time.

A $k$-dimensional covering array is considered universal if it can cover any $k$-dimensional space. A universal covering array is a specific type where all possible spaces are considered, whereas a general covering array only considers a subset of these spaces. This study found that universal general covering arrays exist, meaning they can cover all possible spaces, and it provided a method to construct them. This method revealed that general covering arrays require less elements to cover the required dimensions, less than universal covering arrays, which always consider all possible spaces. This result shows that general covering arrays exist, meaning they can cover all possible dimensions, and it provides a way to construct them. This study also found that general covering arrays approximate a specific lower bound, which means they can cover almost the minimum possible elements required, and the difference becomes negligible as the considered dimensions increase. This study also found that general covering arrays can be constructed by modifying universal covering arrays, which always consider all possible spaces, and the difference between general and universal covering arrays becomes negligible as the considered dimensions increase. This study also found that general covering arrays exist, meaning they can cover all possible dimensions, and it provides a way to construct them. This method showed that general covering arrays exist approximately close to the specific lower bound, meaning they can cover all possible dimensions with very little extra elements required. This study also found that general covering arrays exist approximately close to the specific lower bound, meaning they can cover all possible dimensions with very little extra elements required

In this study, we investigate two variations of a multi-partner game that explores the fundamental aspects of quantum entanglement, where Alice receives random single-qubit measurement instructions and conducts joint measurements on multiple copies of a qubit state prepared by Bob using entanglement. It has been demonstrated that the amount of entanglement in the state determines Alice and Bob's ability to achieve perfect game outcomes with one-qubit query, with fully separable states allowing Bob to win the state-copying game, while at least one bipartite entangled element is required for winning the joint-measurement game. Furthermore, our work reveals that both games can be won using fewer qubits when employing entangled states, and we also discuss a related finding about an unextendible product basis that leads to a nonlocal correlation, thereby challenging conventional definitions of bipartite entanglement.

This research revisits EvoCrash, the inaugural benchmark for benchmarking evolutionary crash prediction models. A key finding contradicts EvoCrash's claim of robustness, suggesting the models are actually vulnerable to failing on difficult program binaries. A proposed explanation for this failure is that EvoCrash's method of selecting input programs via manual testing is insufficient and introduces selection bias. A proposed solution involves replacing the manual method with a more systematic, data-driven approach. The revised approach, when applied to reprocess the EvoCrash dataset, reveals that three of the models no longer meet the benchmark's non-reproductive criteria and also consistently produce non-reproducible results. The revised methods however show a positive correlation with the level of program complexity, the type of program structure, and data size. The analysis suggests that EvoCrash's initial design may not be representative of the broader field of software testing, and that the models' performance is unlikely to improve with the adoption of more advanced testing methods.

Investigating the relationship between a vortex lattice's transition and the structure of superconducting materials, researchers analyzed the momentum dependence in a thin-film high-temperature superconductor, YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-\delta}$. The study involved two transition lines in the vortex lattice that contrasted with the predictions for a d-wave superconductor, particularly near the van Hove singularity where a second superconducting dome emerges. These additional vortices created a transition that surpassed the predicted Kosterlitz-Thouless threshold and led to a significant loss in superconducting properties. The findings suggest that this second transition can be observed in other materials and that the van Hove singularity may be manipulated to enhance high-temperature superconductivity.

The study of sparsity in various aspects of particle physics has emerged as a new and intriguing field of investigation. Utilizing an efficient technique to compute sparsity metrics from events with only three particles, we have analyzed experiments involving the Tevatron and the Large Hadron Collider. By calculating the ratio of the second and third order flow coefficients, derived from sparsity, we have used this metric to understand the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. This discovery is further corroborated by the observation that our sparsity metric correlates strongly with the sixth moment of transverse momentum, as well as with elliptical flow, thus providing an additional event shape correlation. Additionally, we have investigated the use of machine learning algorithms to predict whether an event is single or multi-particle based on the sparsity metric, finding that our approach outperforms other conventional methods. This research has led to a novel method for studying the characteristics of quark-gluon plasma.

We examine how energy and spin structure factors are connected to excitation types in kagome and triangular lattice systems. We establish that these factors can distinguish between configurations of exchangers in kagome lattices and certain spin patterns in triangular lattices, such as the ferromagnetic ground state. We also discuss their utility in analyzing results obtained from quantum simulators.

In contemporary research, the focus has shifted from the concept of significance level to controlling the false discovery rate (FDR). This paper introduces a novel, two-part approach, combining the principles of average treatment effect (ATE) and FDR. Specifically, our proposed methods calculate local false discovery rate (LFDR) to prioritize hypotheses with lower estimated ATE, while also estimating ATE. This targeted approach enables researchers to detect more accurate hypotheses by reducing multiple testing burden. Furthermore, our framework is highly flexible, allowing the incorporation of various statistical tests for continuous and binary outcomes, general linear models, and generalized linear models. This framework is demonstrated through real-world data analysis of the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, specifically examining the relationship between college major selection and future earnings.

The focus of this work lies in the connection between inflationary perturbations and cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature fluctuations as well as other cosmological observables. We establish a straightforward and adaptable framework for examining the CMB, by introducing a basic model of scalar field perturbations. This approach enables the calculation of various CMB statistics, encompassing temperatures fluctuations and their non-Gaussian distributions, across a broad spectrum of curvature profiles, and also extends to other cosmological contexts, such as neutrino asymmetry and large scale structure.

In a modified two Higgs doublet model with an extended scalar sector, the LHCb measurements of magnetic moments for the muon and tau, as well as newly measured magnetic moments for rare b-quark transitions, are in agreement. This model can also explain observed discrepancies in the muon's magnetic moment and predicted W boson mass and strong coupling constant, while maintaining rare b-quark transitions within established limits. Various magnetic moments within the l-quark family are calculated, and potential contributions from rare b-quark transitions, as observable at B-factories, LHCb, and B-accelerators, are explored. The muon's magnetic moment and predicted W boson mass are calculated based on fitted free parameters of the model.

Software development teams struggle to pinpoint where software concepts are used
within a large codebase, especially when multiple developers are involved. To
overcome this challenge, we propose using crowdsourced knowledge to identify concept location.
A key technique in software concept identification is text mining, which relies on software development team members providing metadata to link concepts to line numbers.
However, this process is time-consuming and can be a source of frustration.
To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to software concept identification by leveraging crowdsourced knowledge.
To do this, we first identify the software development task that corresponds to each concept and then design a user-friendly task metadata collection form.
To test the effectiveness of our approach, we applied it to identify the concepts behind four major open-source JavaScript library refactoring tasks on GitHub.
To gather task metadata, we used a task description provided by the GitHub issue or discussion and crowdsourced the information through Stack Overflow.
The results indicate that our approach successfully identifies concept location and that the task metadata collected through crowdsourcing is of high quality.

We investigate the potential of neural methods in identifying fabricated dialogue by examining the Dialogue Generation vs. Dialogue Editing dilemma. Both processes contribute to a natural language ultimate dialogue but offer distinct insights into detecting fabricated dialogue. To this end, we introduce the Neural Entrainment Distance (NED) metric, capturing the ultimate dialogue's speaker interactions in latent space. Combined with NED, we create a hybrid classifier to increase the efficiency and precision of detecting fabricated dialogue. Our experiments on the Reddit Relationship Advice Shared Decision Dataset reveal that the hybrid classifier achieves an 84.4% F1 score, outperforming state-of-the-art models that use either dialogue generation or editing approaches.

The BPT diagrams, based on emission line ratios, serve as a standard for classifying galaxy spectra into star-forming, AGN, and other categories. The lines used are typically narrow, but a new approach employs both narrow and broad emission lines from AGNs to create a novel BPT diagram. The process begins by identifying narrow and broad emission line profiles, then utilizes narrow lines to determine the galaxy's star-forming status. The ratio between the full width at half maximum of the emission line and the galaxy's stellar velocity dispersion is calculated, and if a galaxy is star-forming, its classification is based on the H{\sc\alpha} or [O{\sc iii}] emission line's full width at half maximum velocity dispersion ratio. Otherwise, it is classified according to the broad emission line spectrum's [O{\sc ii}]/H{\sc\alpha} ratio. Applying this method to the SDSS DR16 dataset, researchers found that 13\% of galaxies previously classified as AGNs are actually star-forming, indicating a significant contamination issue. Furthermore, they established a relationship between the [O{\sc iii}]/H{\sc\alpha} flux ratio and z for the entire galaxy population, indicating an increase in [O{\sc iii}] flux with increasing z.

This paper presents the Co-occurrence Action Parsing (C.A.P.) algorithm, which outperforms current state-of-the-art open-action-action segmentation approaches by utilizing skeleton-only data. C.A.P.'s design is based on simplifying action segmentation to an action recognition task and is grounded in the concept that action boundaries are either start or end points and are difficult to determine without clear action recognition. C.A.P.'s first step is an action boundary end-point detection system that utilizes pre-trained action recognizers to identify action boundaries and then refines the results by using the pre-trained action recognizers to identify action boundaries and then uses an action parsing algorithm to identify action boundaries and then uses an action parsing algorithm to identify action boundaries and then uses an action parsing algorithm to identify action boundaries. In experiments that used three publicly available action segmentation datasets, C.A.P.'s performance is significantly better than current state-of-the-art open-action-action segmentation algorithms.

Using a complete set of diagrams, the relative production rates for the decay processes of a set of states are calculated, and then applied to scenarios where some parameters are unknown. This method is used to examine specific relationships in non-leptonic decay processes of a subset of $\Lambda_b^to$ processes, and also to test the parameters of the Standard Model by examining the ratio of certain $\Lambda_b^to$ decay ratios that involve charmonium resonances, specifically the J/$\psi$. By comparing these values to theoretical predictions that suggest no CP violation occurs, a discrepancy is found, and a potential explanation for this discrepancy is proposed, suggesting a particular pattern of the standard model's CKM matrix parameters. This proposal is then tested with related processes involving a bottomless quark and a charmed quark.

Our investigation examines the impact of varying feedback types on students' code coverage and programming achievement. Through the analysis of two experiments involving a total of 212 students using game-based learning, we discovered that students who received hints and implemented them achieved higher code coverage compared to their counterparts who received no feedback. Conversely, students who received and applied debugging assistance from their instructors tended to earn better grades on average. The findings suggest that feedback is most effective when students actively engage with it. The results also reveal that incorporating hints in programming exercises can boost students' code coverage and promote deeper exploration of their code, while instructors should balance coverage enhancement with fostering debugging skills to effectively improve students' grades.

Since its inception, domain adaptation has been a prominent area of research in machine learning. The significant impact of this field is hindered by the substantial source data annotation requirements that current methods face. The unlabelled data utilization in domain adaptation methods such as contrastive learning and pseudo-labeling has significant limitations. The paper presents an innovative approach that circumvents these limitations by leveraging pseudo-labels and contrastive learning in an self-supervised setting. The proposed method, dubbed Self-UDA, employs an unsupervised representation learning technique to generate an unbiased domain-invariant representation, and its effectiveness is showcased through experiments on image and speech datasets, yielding superior or comparable results to existing state-of-the-art methods while greatly reducing the data annotation burden.

This study examines the transient thermal behavior of a gas core reactor, specifically one that utilizes helium and an liquid fluoride salt. By incorporating the effects of pressure on the reactor's thermal-hydraulic and neutronic characteristics, the research provides an in-depth analysis through a detailed two-dimensional two-flow-loop simulation. The simulation includes precise models for the helium and salt, accurately capturing their thermophysical properties. With a commercially available solver, LiSe 2.0, and a representative 2D reactor model, consisting of two separate channels, the researchers explored various coupled thermal-hydraulic and neutronic transients triggered by control rod insertions. The transient scenarios explored include both normal and abnormal operating conditions, such as the removal of core reactivity due to control rod movement, a sudden valve opening in one flow loop, and the simultaneous valve opening and control rod insertion, all of which involved different initial reactor states. The results revealed significant time-varying reactor power and fluid flow, temperature, density, and void fraction fluctuations, offering valuable insights into the behavior of gas core reactors during both routine and emergency situations.

Building upon a prior work that developed neural networks using only event data, 
we extended the neural network architecture to utilize not only event data but 
also experiment's prior detector knowledge as additional input channels. The 
architect's knowledge of the detector is encoded as a two-dimensional map, which 
is combined with the multi-channel event data to generate the final neural 
network output. In this instance, we trained the neural network to locate muon 
tracks in simulated data, which were generated using Geant4 and ROOT. The 
results indicate that these algorithms can achieve excellent muon localization 
without any training data and potentially offer real-world applications. The 
code implementing these algorithms is available on GitHub.

Our research involves a comparative analysis of synthetic spectra generated using various TiO line lists and a choice of atmospheric models for a subset of observations from the James Webb Space Telescope on a specific atmosphere. We compared spectra produced using the TiO-IMOD line lists, the TiO Burrows list, and a combination of both, which were integrated into the software FastNav. Our analysis revealed that the Burrows list has a notable impact on the results, with significant discrepancies in the spectral features it produces. While the spectra from the TiO-IMOD and Burrows lists have distinct patterns, they do not align with the actual spectra we analyzed. However, when we created hybrid spectral models using the transits and eclipse data, we found that these combined models provide a more accurate representation that is consistent with our observations.

This paper examines the effect of Annotated Logic Programs' groundings on the generation of answer set expansions and discusses the integration of recursive aggregate annotations in the process. The analysis compares two existing grounding methods for recursive aggregates, highlighting their distinct features, and evaluates a novel combination of both approaches to address unresolved cases. The study of recursive aggregate grounding in logic programs is a crucial aspect of answer set programming, with significant implications for semantics.

The theoretical framework for thermodynamic processes, based on abstract theoretical models, is the theoretical foundation of thermodynamic theories independent of their macroscopic or quantum nature. In this paper, the relationship between thermodynamic processes and the work they produce is the focus and a general thermodynamic process model is derived, in line with the first thermodynamic law. This model reveals that the change in a system's internal energy is equivalent to the change in its work-capability. In addition, a specific type of transformation, called thermal transformation, is identified and demonstrated to be the most efficient mechanism to convert work into heat within certain theoretical models. In order to obtain the most efficient method to extract work, a broader class of transformations is considered, encompassing both extracting work and dissipating it. A specific transformation, called an isentropic transformation, is identified and demonstrated to be the most efficient mechanism to convert and dissipate work within certain theoretical models.

This study introduces a novel approach for computing the relationship between joint and marginal distributions of discrete and continuous data using the Cramer-von Mises statistic. We represent empirical joint and marginal distributions as random variables and leverage molecular decomposition to express their moments. We propose an estimator of the relationship measure $\phi$ between data attributes based on these moments, and demonstrate its applicability to information measures such as mutual information and total variation distance. Using Efron's bootstrap method, we calculate the required moments and show that the proposed estimator can consistently estimate target values, and validate its performance through sample experiments.

The count of common stochastic trends in financial data is crucial in understanding market movements and has significant implications for portfolio management, a topic extensively explored in academic literature. A novel asymptotic estimator has been developed to detect the count of common stochastic trends in financial time series data, characterized by two-dimensional stability and potentially exhibiting heavy tails. Through a series of numerical experiments, it has been demonstrated that the estimator's accuracy is largely unaffected by the tail weight but does experience a decrease in precision with smaller sample sizes. Notably, in controlled scenarios, the estimator's precision is comparable to other established estimators. A practical application of this estimator to real-world financial data has also been presented.

We utilize an innovative method based on quantum finite field verification to construct a family of explicit quantum codes from a left-right Cayley complex, which serves as the penalty term in the quantum code's design. As the size of the complex increases, so do the code's parameters, allowing for arbitrary improvements in size, codeword count, and error tolerance. Furthermore, our approach surpasses previously existing constructions, including those by Kalai and Levkin, in both asymptotic efficiency and overall performance. We also briefly explore the concept of a quantum counterpart to Kalai's constructions.

In this work, we explore the distance-$r$ dominating set problem within a distributed environment on a network graph where nodes and edges represent connections between graph vertices. Our approach involves a randomized algorithm that finds a near-optimal solution on graphs where the network has low depth and communicates between connected vertices. On graphs where the network has a specific structure called treewidth, our proposed algorithm is deterministic and achieves the best possible result. Additionally, on graphs where the network has a specific structure called minor excluded, our proposed algorithm is near-optimal and uses an adaptive measure of rounds.

In higher-order topological insulators with weak electronic disorder, 
(R)TIs and (W)TI classes exhibit two separate gaps within the bulk of the
spectrum: a disorder-induced "bulk" gap and an intrinsic gap. Similarly, edge
states are bounded by R and W mobility gaps, which arise from the disorder-induced
splitting of intrinsic topological modes. When the disorder strength is low, 
individual, intrinsic edge states remain within their respective R and W gaps.
Our research explores the impact of disorder on the split topological states in
two-dimensional H3KTI classes, utilizing various models of intrinsic and disorder
Hamiltonians. The findings indicate that disorder-induced splitting is more 
sensitive to the form of intrinsic topological states, but not to the type of
disorder. We also analyze the relationship between the disorder-induced gap and
the intrinsic band gap in the clean limit.

A study was conducted to search for rare, long-lived charginos produced in pairs, which decay into stable neutrons along with other particles. The investigation focused on areas of the supersymmetry parameter space with minimal background interference, specifically examining charginos produced alongside the lightest neutralino, and into a variety of final states including a variety of visible final states. The experiment found no background events in data collected at high energies, and as a result, placed limits on the production of compressed charginos with masses close to that of the neutralino, which have masses of 1100 GeV or less. The limits have an estimated production cross-section of less than 1 picobarn, and specifically exclude charginos with a mass difference greater than 25 GeV and a lifetime between 0.1 nanoseconds and 0.1 seconds, and also exclude charginos with a mass difference greater than 40 GeV and a lifetime of 0.1 seconds in an additional analysis.

Our approach, named GeMMer, leverages the properties of geometric scene structure to perform light field rendering with minimal input views. We achieve this goal by employing geometric constraints to guide the learning of scene geometry representations and differentiable light field rendering, thus producing visually accurate and geometrically plausible geometry. Furthermore, we extend our method to tackle rendering challenges associated with occluded and transparent objects. Evaluations on both synthetic test datasets and real-world data demonstrate that GeMMer outperforms existing methods in terms of image quality and accuracy, while also requiring fewer input images. The code and datasets for GeMMer are publicly available.

Using speckle interferometry, researchers conducted high-resolution observations on a sample of 121 nearby dwarf stars with V magnitudes ranging from 6 to 14, all of which had previously been identified as multiple systems or subsystems. The newly acquired data from the Intermediate Angular Resolution Interferometer at the Palomar Transient Factory yielded a 1.06 arcsecond field of view and offered unique opportunities to capture and analyze sub-pairs within systems of triple and higher-order multiples. The study yielded 188 new binary and triple systems and excluded 20, resulting in comprehensive relative astrometry for 108 pairs with separation ranges between 1.1 and 6.0 arcseconds. The new data significantly expanded the existing relative astrometry of 100 pairs, providing a foundation for deriving precise orbital solutions for 11 binaries and refining the orbital parameters of 40 systems. Additionally, the study identified a potential substellar companion in a previously unknown pair, resulting from a new speckle detection. The complete catalog of observations, including 288 pairs with 21 new triples, is available for reference.

The chiral OPE of self-dual gravity is utilized to link its associativity to the chiral structure of an chiral theory, as well as to the self-dual component of the Kerr black hole scattering amplitudes. The level-four Weyl theory is identified as the simplest model exhibiting self-dual gravity, enabling us to verify that the chiral OPE product is associative and that the resulting self-dual scattering amplitudes correspond to those derived by Kerr in 1963.

Radio observations of the shock revealed two distinct regions of emission. Above 300 MHz, the shock's leading edge produced a type II radio burst, which ended in a type III outburst. The shock's initial phase, where the shock's front emitted a type II outburst, was found to emit at lower frequencies. The shock's two-phase structure is consistent with the interplanetary shock's observations. The shock's emission mechanism is attributed to the interaction between a solar jet plasma and pre-existing magnetic fields. The shock's initial phase, where the jet plasma interacts with magnetic fields, is consistent with the initial type II phase. A novel type of violation in flavor and CP is introduced within the framework of the general two Higgs doublet model, a variation of the minimal supersymmetric model, by incorporating a non-diagonal soft SUSY breaking term involving the extra Higgs doublet. A non-zero term in this variation leads to off-diagonal squark masses in the first generation of quarks, thereby creating non-diagonal gluino-higgsino-flavor changing interactions and loop-induced b s gamma transition. In this model, the mixing between h and Z bosons is also possible, while lepton violations are predicted to occur. A numerical analysis of various two Higgs doublet models within this framework is conducted, focusing on how these models affect particle decays and violations in B mesons, while also exploring potential contributions to C P violation in b s gamma transitions and lepton violations. Results from this study are compared with theoretical predictions for future collider observables, including the Higgs boson decay into tau and muon leptons, as well as the muon anomalous magnetic moment.

A novel rotary vortex system's evolution is initially explored and its emergence within the framework of vorticity equations is demonstrated. The proposed system's utility in developing numerical algorithms for three-dimensional fluid flow computation using a finite difference approach on a Cartesian grid is then showcased.

Gene expression data analysis is a complex process, but it's crucial to identify the relevant variables for accurate predictions. In order to streamline this process and improve model performance, we propose the relevance learning framework, which can be applied in two contexts - the global search for predictive variables across all data, and the local search to identify variables specific to certain subgroups in the data. Our research focuses on the global search context and demonstrates its effectiveness using simulated and real data, particularly in gene expression data over time. By incorporating time-dependent relevance learning, we can accurately identify the predictive variables across time points, or the variables present at specific time points, making our method a valuable addition to the existing relevance learning framework.

A study proves that a given linear time-invariant system can be designed such that, when used with a specific type of neural network in partially observable environments, the network's internal states fail to effectively represent the optimal strategy for decision-making, given the observed data. This line-invariant system can also be adapted so that the network's internal states cause the entire system to become unstable. Consequently, both the failure of neural networks to represent optimal strategies and their potential contribution to system instability are shown to be inherent limitations, rather than just a result of suboptimal parameter settings.

The detection of actions within a single video clip is a significant challenge in computer vision. In our approach, we address this challenge by combining self-attention mechanisms with Graph Convolutional Networks. These components enable us to capture spatial relationships between key frames and temporal information within the entire clip. Additionally, we incorporate spatial attention to highlight important regions in each frame. Our proposed method, GirTV, outperforms state-of-the-art action detection techniques on two benchmark datasets named *JHMDB* and *Something-Something V2*. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub.

Successful image copy detection strategies rely on combining low-level features like image patches, high-level deep features, and geometric constraints. Notably, deep features and spatial constraints have driven the most impactful advancements in copy detection performance over the past decade. In contrast, the utilization of low-level features has not received sufficient attention, leading to the underestimation of their efficacy. Our study demonstrates that the efficacy of traditional image copy detection image patch methods has been significantly overlooked, leading to the underestimation of their performance in modern contexts.

We investigate a variety of regularity issues for both linear and nonlinear parabolic equations, which are subject to either Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions as well as initial conditions. These problems arise from combining spatial and temporal regularity estimates for equations like the following:

$\begin{cases}
u_t-A(Du,D^Xu)=f&\text{in } \Omega\times(0,T),\\
u=0&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),
\end{cases}$

$\begin{cases}
u_t-A(Du,D^Xu)=f&\text{in } \Omega\times(0,T),\\
\frac{\partial Du}{\partial n}=0&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),
\end{cases}$

where $A$ is a given function that depends on the first derivative of $u$ and the second derivative of $u$, and the problem is defined within a space-time cylinder that includes the time interval from $0$ to $T$ and a bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$. The problem either involves setting $u$ to $0$ on the boundary of $\Omega$ or to a function $g$ on both the boundary of $\Omega$ and time, and we also consider the case where the second derivative of $u$ in the normal direction is zero.

In the absence of a magnetic field and at zero temperature, quark matter exhibits a gap in energy and displays zero spin polarization. However, upon the introduction of a strong magnetic field, it transforms into a state of spin-polarized color superconductivity. A theoretical framework has been developed to describe this phenomenon, specifically as a state of spin-polarized triplet superconductivity in the two-flavor triplet, characterized by the $T_{1C}$ pairing. Research indicates the emergence of an energetically favorable, polarized state below a critical magnetic field, which is not significantly influenced by the strength of the magnetic interaction or the strength of the coupling. Furthermore, the critical magnetic field is negligible compared to typical strong magnetic fields, and the superconducting gap is lower than the isospin-polarized gap, which exists at finite temperatures.

A paper has been published to address the challenge of integrating Differential Privacy into Federated Learning algorithms, focusing on the impact of data updates on clients and server aggregation. The research also considers how the Privacy budget is affected and provides tests for generated data against General Distributions. Additionally, experiments on real-world scenarios test the effectiveness of FL-DP algorithms on both real and artificial attacks, as well as comparisons to traditional ML and FP methods.

The region of Taurus-Auriga-Perseus in the Galaxy is home to low-mass protostars that emit powerful radiation, creating bright H2 molecules in the far-ultraviolet spectrum. These fluorescent emissions are an important component of the region's overall far-ultraviolet intensity, making it a valuable tool for detecting young stars. Using data from the FUV Hubble Space Telescope, this study provides a detailed map of H2 emissions and identifies three distinct clouds, which are separated by ionizing radiation from the low-mass stars in the region. These clouds show a direct relationship with young stars, which emit radiation that ionize the H2 molecules, causing them to glow. Evidence of ionization by these low-mass stars, as well as cosmic rays, is found in the observed spectral lines. The shape of the H2 clouds, which are flat and perpendicular to the direction of ionizing radiation, suggests that dust dust extinction and gas pressure are the primary factors influencing their shape. These findings are consistent with simple theoretical models of ionizing radiation from low-mass stars.

Table extraction from document images is enhanced by Graph Neural Networks, which enable the detection of individual cells and the preservation of hierarchical structures, all without the need for training. We present a proposed algorithm incorporating GNNs for table extraction from document images, accompanied by a detailed explanation and performance evaluation on two distinct datasets.

Inspired by the concept of dynamic games of incomplete information, our research introduces an intelligence metric that evaluates an agent's capacity to learn face recognition across diverse scenarios. This new metric is grounded in the game theory, where each player's payoff depends on actions taken by others, and it is measured by the game value. Unlike traditional neural networks that achieve high accuracy on specific datasets but fail in general scenarios, lower-level agents with basic intelligence tend to exhibit poor performance due to their misunderstanding of key features. Conversely, advanced players demonstrate superior generalization capabilities. The game value, representing the average payoff, is maximized by an agent's optimal action known as the game's maximin strategy.

This research explores how reducing population density in urban areas can contribute to more accurate and refined measurements. By applying a Gaussian distribution to estimate the spatial footprint of individuals, we developed a method to calculate the total area covered by each urban cluster. Using this technique, we trained a deep learning model to predict population sizes, achieving significant improvements when tested in two scenarios. In one experiment, using only publicly available information, the model improved predictions by around 10%. In another, by incorporating the estimated footprint area along with night light intensity data, the model achieved an even greater improvement of approximately 20%.

This paper introduces an enhanced version of the $k$-anonymity static filter known as LSEF that strikes a balance between avoiding false negatives without compromising on efficiency in terms of storage or processing speed. In contrast to conventional static filters that categorize queries into either $k$-anonymity-compliant or non-compliant categories, LSEF incorporates case-specific optimizations to ensure that certain queries that can be $k$-anonymity-compliant in certain contexts are not incorrectly dismissed. This is achieved by considering query tree structures in the context of schema hierarchies during filter construction. LSEF is versatile and can be adapted to various generalization functions. We illustrate the effectiveness of LSEF through its application in two different generalization functions.

In the case of ultracold bosonic mixtures composed of two hyperfine states, both in the same spatial mode, a non-equilibrium phase transition occurs upon introducing a dissipative coupling between them. This novel phenomenon, involving the ultrafast onset of a quantum pendulum-like instability, relies on accurately tracking the time-evolution of atom-molecule conversions during the initial period. Achieving this requires precise lattice depths and atom number counts, both of which can be experimentally obtained. Our research demonstrates that accounting for atom-molecule conversions aids in predicting critical lattice parameters and also sheds light on the early stages of an autonomous pendulum-like instability.

A novel multi-phase multi-resolution SPH method, the second of its kind, is presented in this research. The method employs a novel multi-phase formulation, incorporating two distinct components: an interaction-particle-based pressure, utilizing a high-order kernel to mitigate low-density issues, and the Taylor-expansion-based pressure for high-density scenarios. Utilizing a pre-processing technique to assign particles unique resolution phases and implementing a kernel refinement procedure to adjust resolution phases among particles within an interacting radius, this approach effectively overcomes challenges associated with voids, phase separation, and multi-resolution transitions. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through a series of test cases, and key parameters are identified and analyzed.

Quantum machine learning, which leverages quantum algorithms to enhance machine learning efficiency, has the potential to provide exponential speedup in specific tasks. One such task is the widely-used K-means clustering algorithm, where we have developed a K-means variant with improved efficiency. Our approach involves using a data storage method with $\Theta(n)$ query complexity, yielding speedup over classical methods. However, we have also demonstrated that the proposed quantum K-means has clustering performance slightly lower than classical methods. Notably, the performance difference diminishes as input dimension increases or the number of features per sample decreases, ultimately achieving identical performance in certain scenarios.

Recent advancements in neural speech synthesis techniques have led to impressive progress, yet simple models reliant on a text-based pitch representation are prone to inaccuracies when dealing with complex and variable pitch contours. To address this challenge, our study investigates the effects of enhancing training datasets with artificially altered pitch information and the implications of one-hot pitch encoding on the speech synthesis system's ability to control pitch. Our approach, based on the FastSpeech2 model, involves modifying datasets to include pitch-shuffled and pitch-reversed speech samples. Our analysis and experimental results confirm that training with modified pitch information enhances the speech synthesis model's ability to control pitch and generates more natural speech.

Our proposal for efficient spatiotemporal object-centric reasoning involves using a short video sequence and employing contrastive loss to differentiate unique and distinct object trajectories within a video timeline, thus enabling focused attention on singular object sequences. Unlike existing approaches relying on complex reinforcement learning-based planning methods, we achieve accurate prediction of object movements through straightforward regression techniques. To validate the effectiveness of contrastive loss in object-centric reasoning, we introduce the Small Object Reasoning Challenge dataset and compare the object-centric prediction models against state-of-the-art baselines. The results show that our method, incorporating contrastive loss, surpasses baseline models in prediction accuracy while significantly reducing training time. The proposed approach can be easily extended to other state-of-the-art models, as demonstrated through our integration of contrastive loss with the MiT model, yielding superior results on benchmark datasets. The proposed method, referred to as contrastive MiT, achieves a result of 56.8% on the TCR dataset and 61.3% on the TORD dataset, outperforming the tuned MiT model. The code for contrastive MiT is publicly available on GitHub.

This paper examines the connection between W boson polarization measurements and standard charged-current Drell-Yan process observables within the context of parton distribution function (PDF) simulations. Utilizing data from W boson decays at large rapidities collected by ATLAS in 2015, researchers investigated the correlation between the transverse momentum distributions of lepton pairs and specific x-values in PDF functions. These x-values correspond to the fraction of momentum carried by the interacting partons. Results from ATLAS showed that altering the shape of these PDF functions to influence the transverse momentum distribution of leptons also impacted the W boson polarization. This interaction demonstrates that optimizing the standard chemical potential to fit data on charged-current Drell-Yan processes would lead to discrepancies in the transverse momentum distribution data. This study demonstrates that PDF function simulations affect W boson polarization measurements and emphasizes the importance of accounting for such interactions in the assessment of these measurements' uncertainties.

Users of telepresence robots may experience visual and interactive differences between visual and navigation aspects, which can be overlooked in evaluation methods primarily reliant on surveys. To better understand and compare these experiences, we employed an experimental method to gather data on users' perceptions while operating telepresence robots via two distinct interfaces. Our results indicate that users' visual and interactive experiences vary significantly, and we provide insights into the factors contributing to these discrepancies.

Bayesian machine learning models, specifically fully and partially supervised hierarchical Gaussian process models, are used to create probabilistic maps of global plant functionality. The impact of soil nitrogen concentration on plant size is found to be significant, and as a result, models incorporating nitrogen data are found to provide more precise predictions, particularly in lower levels of the model hierarchy. The performance of these models, when hierarchical structures are not employed, is notably degraded. The ability of these models to predict functionality in environments with limited data is crucial, and they are found to be versatile and effective tools for monitoring the state of the Earth's biosphere and forecasting its future functionality.

The enduring appeal of the social deduction game, Mafia, lies in its seemingly endless replayability, despite the numerous analyses it has received over the years. We conducted an in-depth, data-driven investigation to uncover the underlying patterns of optimal play in Mafia 2, by $\lambda$-mix play. Our study, based on an extensive dataset of 20 million game results, provides new insights into the effects of various game parameters, such as game length, Mafia and Seer counts, and initial player positions. Our analysis reveals the significance of these factors and sheds light on the essential qualities of optimal play, such as the Mafia's need for coordination and communication, and the importance of communication for successful Hunter's Hunt strategy execution.

A theoretical model has been developed to examine the interaction between multiple giant planets and their mass distribution during accretion from a single disk. We have analyzed a system of three planets, located at 10 AU, 20 AU, and 30 AU respectively, which have masses of 10 Earth masses. Through interactions with gas and each other, these planets can experience migration, while their masses can be influenced by disk interactions. We have studied the relationship between convergence times for mass equalization and the parameters of the planet-disk system. We found that inner planets tend to have lower disk interaction coefficients and higher mass growth rates, which can lead to a flux deficit and a decrease in the available solid surface density. We found that a 10 AU planet experiences mass equalization in 1.5 million years, while a 20 AU planet undergoes the same process in 3 million years. We observed a linear relationship between the disk interaction coefficient and the time required for mass equalization. We propose that multiple giant planets can coexist in a planet-disk interaction model, which can explain their mass distribution and orbital characteristics.

We have investigated thermal transport in single-wall carbon nanotubes using various techniques, including single-tube measurements, Raman spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations. Our focus lies on understanding thermal transport mechanisms at high temperatures, which has significant implications for the design of nanoscale devices. Raman spectroscopy revealed that thermal transport in armchair nanotubes occurs primarily through phonon conduction, whereas electron conduction becomes dominant at lower temperatures. Notably, phonon conduction exhibits temperature dependence similar to that of bulk silicon, suggesting armchair nanotubes could serve as effective thermal conductors for silicon-based microelectronics. Additionally, our simulations indicate electron conduction remains relatively unaffected by temperature up to 400 K.

The traditional fuzzy k-means algorithm has a drawback of being overly confident when assigning objects to clusters. To address this issue, the authors have developed the α-fuzzy k-means algorithm, which modifies the objective function by incorporating entropy terms in the objective function. This modification allows the introduction of an index 'α', representing the confidence level of each object's cluster membership. Consequently, the 'α' parameter enables the 'α-fuzzy k-means' clustering technique to be versatile and adaptable, particularly suitable when the 'α' values are predetermined.

A novel algorithm for training mixture-of-experts models is introduced, focusing on accurately estimating key parameters from data. Each iteration involves a two-step process: first, a mixture component generates predictions, then an expert component refines them. Experimental evaluation on synthetic data sets reveals that this algorithm outperforms traditional methods in estimating parameter values,consuming less computational time.
