Utilizing cutting-edge methods, researchers have moved away from conventional approaches that heavily rely on explicit mathematical formulas and instead turned toward techniques utilizing implicit representation and neural networks. A key advantage of these new methods lies in their ability to analyze complex, high-dimensional nonlinear systems, particularly those that operate near equilibrium states. This concept is further exemplified through investigations into the dynamics of frequency and voltage fluctuations within power grids, examining how secondary and primary control mechanisms influence one another and ultimately, the stability of the grid.

Cyber-physical systems encompass systems with interconnected physical and computational parts, which can be categorized into control and communication layers based on their distinct properties. Within these systems, differential equations model the control part, which operates at a high processing speed and uses precise physical methods. Conversely, the communication part transmits data over discrete time intervals using a packet-based protocol. To bridge this communication gap, data is sampled based on event triggers. By employing Markovian analysis, researchers examined the behavior of networked control systems. Nevertheless, such models often come with computational complexities that limit their ability to analyze larger systems. Therefore, researchers focused on identifying conditions that ensure stability within these systems without necessitating complex computations. They developed simplified models that approximate large-scale networked control systems and analyzed whether these systems maintain stability when individual components are stable. Furthermore, researchers analyzed the behavior of individual parts of the system during transient periods.

Blazars, characterized by intense electromagnetic radiation, offer a unique opportunity to study the polarized emission of this radiation and, in turn, gain insights into the astrophysical processes at play within their complex environments. To gain a deeper understanding of these processes, researchers aim to develop advanced polarimetry techniques for blazar observations. This paper outlines a comprehensive framework for blazar polarization analysis and presents predictive models for UV and X-ray polarized emissions based on the expected geometry of these sources. A simulation framework for modeling blazar polarimetry is also described, opening up new avenues for the development of polarimetry in blazar observations.

The properties of high-order replica hessian matrices for spin glass models with randomly disordered structures were analyzed systematically and represented through random matrix theory's spectral form parameters. Models with distinct landscape configurations, specifically those with progressively replicated hessian structures as replica numbers increase, were categorized into two distinct types based on their scale behavior: one that exhibits a linear relationship with replica numbers and another that plateaus at a certain value. These theoretical predictions were validated against actual spin glass models that exhibit varying complexity levels and random spectral form parameters. Models that exhibit a linear relationship tend to have simpler structures, whereas those that exhibit a plateau indicate the presence of multiple energy minima within the system.

Our research examines the performance of online methods in detecting and recognizing distinct symmetric states, particularly when they share a consistent level of overlap. Notably, for states that are gradually similar, the best methods perform poorly, taking exponentially longer to process as N increases. In contrast, for states that are gradually distinct, an optimal online scheme achieves a performance comparable to its offline counterpart, effectively minimizing errors. These findings are highly relevant in scenarios involving the identification of DNA sequences and other processes where incremental analysis is necessary.

The masses derived from the light meson spectra serve as a benchmark in constructing a model framework for calculating light baryon masses according to QCD. A specific model, incorporating both light quark and heavy charm or bottom flavors, has been formulated in an $SU(3)$ framework. This model, developed from a Lagrangian, captures the intricate quark interactions within a $U(3)$ potential, enabling the simulation of both light baryons and heavy charm/bottom baryons. When applied, the model model recovers the experimental mass spectrum for octet baryons with remarkable accuracy. Furthermore, it also generates a well-ordered mass spectrum for various baryons containing charm or bottom quarks.

We've identified robust meridional flow signals within the sun's deep interior by analyzing long-term acoustic wave patterns, specifically their travel times. This discovery is significant as it reveals the presence of strong horizontal currents within the sun, particularly at its outer edge. These currents are characterized by intense variability and are distinct from those found in the sun's surface layer. The found signals match previously discovered time-varying features in the sun's acoustic wave patterns. This discovery provides new insights into the sun's internal structure, particularly its rotation and magnetic activity. Our analysis shows that the sun's internal rotation rate is influenced by these strong horizontal flows. Additionally, our research suggests that the sun's internal structure is more complex than previously thought, with multiple strong currents interacting to shape the sun's internal dynamics.

Magnetic fields, particularly when present in the early universe, significantly influence fluctuations and waves, directly affecting the formation of cosmic structures and possibly the wave primordials that will be detected by future detectors. A magnetic field, especially when it's primordial and present in the early universe, can strongly impact the fluctuations of other components, which in turn affects fluctuations and waves itself, leading to altered cosmic spectrum properties. In this study, we investigate how a magnetic field, particularly when it's primordial and present in the early universe, affects other components' fluctuations and waves. Specifically, it can cause fluctuations to transfer to smaller scales and waves to amplify its amplitude by approximately 10% or less, which in turn leads to altered oscillations in other components. In addition, this influence results in both amplified and damped oscillations in other components, which in turn leads to differences in cosmic spectrum properties.

The four-dimensional (4D) light field (LF) image, comprising multiple sub-images captured from varied perspectives, presents an inherent irregularity in spatial information. Traditional methods that compress each sub-image independently, ignoring the inherent disparity among them, often result in inferior performance compared to a single conventional image. To address this, we propose a novel 4D LF image compression framework centered around two core components: a disparity-aided model and a sub-image-specific entropy coding module. The disparity-aided model leverages the inherent geometric disparity in the LF to enhance initial compression and reduce inter-view inconsistency. Furthermore, our entropy coding module employs neural entropy estimation and arithmetic coding to optimize bit allocation based on the probability distribution of compressed residual images. Evaluation results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed scheme in reducing compression rate while outperforming state-of-the-art methods significantly, with an average sum of absolute error improvement of 1.6 dB and a sum of absolute error reduction exceeding 8.5% at equivalent distortion levels.

We address the challenge of cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) by leveraging an query translation approach. Building upon recent advances in zero-shot translation pre-training, we initiate the exploration of CLIR as a semi-interactive task. From the user's perspective, this involves providing input in one language and receiving a matching document or result from a system not matching the input language. We develop a framework that utilizes a pre-trained language model for language representation, combined with a simple but effective mechanism that leverages multiple language representations to enhance CLIR performance. We assess the efficacy of this mechanism with both synthetic and real-world datasets, achieving CLIR accuracy improvements of around 10% in support language pairs where the input and output languages differ.

We introduce a novel spatial model that leverages fine-grained, demographically-oriented data from the US Census. This model, however, poses a challenge due to the high level of noise and limited sample size. To address this issue, we have developed an inference method that relies on a variational approximation technique. Utilizing this method, we can estimate demographic data with high precision, while also accounting for subtle variations within neighborhoods. Our model's capabilities are showcased through its application to the analysis of racial composition in US cities. This involves estimating demographic data with high resolution, and using this information to predict the number of individuals requiring a particular service, such as a pediatrician. Our model is available for download at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/alextk/CSM.

This paper introduces the concept of quantum memory gambling, where past outcomes influence future events. We examine the quantum memory betting model and discover that holding onto free quantum memory can be equally effective as investing in it. We also find that, unlike classical gambling, there is no single optimal strategy; instead, multiple strategies can be combined to achieve maximum returns. Furthermore, our research reveals that these optimal strategies adapt to changing market conditions, allowing the returns to remain in a specific range regardless of the outcomes' correlations.

We have examined the discrepancy between the predictions of density functional theory and Green's function methods for the quasiparticle band structure of GaAs, AlGaAs, and their superlattices. Our results indicate that the discrepancy arises from the fact that the core-valence contribution in the dipole approximation is not fully canceled out. Additionally, we have compared predictions made by the GW approximation and the W0 approximation and found that the W0 approximation does not accurately represent the quasiparticle energy in the band gap region. However, we have discovered that the W0 approximation does capture the essential features of the GW-concept in the excitonic bound-state spectrum, including the convergence of bound-state energies to zero coupling. Our findings also suggest that the W0 approximation can accurately describe the many-body screening of bound states in the band gap region. Nevertheless, we have demonstrated through the examination of the superlattice gap states that the W0 approximation fails to capture the GW-concept regarding the screening of these states.

The Study for the Muon and Muonless Decays of $\Sigma^+$ (SMMuM) has a unique setup, consisting of a large-volume detector and a dedicated beam-line, specifically designed to study $\Sigma^+$ decay properties. Located at Fermilab's Main Injector, the SMMuM detector is positioned 65.6 meters away from the beam-target interaction point. In a search for $\Sigma^+$ decays into a proton and a $\pi^0$, utilizing the detector's photomultiplier-tuned for gamma detection, data from a 2018 beam-run will be analyzed. This study is expected to achieve a sensitivity for the $\Sigma^+$ partial branching fraction, reaching an order of $10^{-5}$ or lower.

Our research focuses on the characteristics of turbulent magnetohydrodynamic flows within a rotating, acicular protoplanetary disk. By analyzing the mid-plane and upper layers separately, we developed an approximate analytical model. This model considers the effects of turbulent flow on the mid-plane and upper layers, as well as the impact of magnetic fields on the disk's properties, such as turbulence, density, and vertical thickness. Our study reveals that the mid-plane and upper layers exhibit distinct characteristics, with magnetic pressure playing a significant role in the disk's behavior. Our analytical predictions align well with numerical simulations. Our research has significant implications for understanding the formation and evolution of planetary systems, particularly in relation to the distribution of solids and magnetic fields.

We've created a comprehensive approach to designing Adaptive Coherent Detectors (ADCs) and optimized it using sophisticated modeling. Our algorithm generalizes the dispersion model, allowing for more accurate optimization in real-world environments. Our research analyzed two models, one by Pearce and another by RAE, and discovered that the Pearce model can lead to inaccuracies in the ADC's performance in the blue spectrum range. To mitigate this issue, we proposed a way to adjust the ADC's weights to account for atmospheric dispersion, leading to a more accurate representation. Our simulations revealed that a 10% error in group index can be corrected, and we found that the ADC's performance is more robust in the near-infrared range. Our results show that a more complex modeling approach can be used to achieve better performance in real-world environments.

The conventional approach to modeling time series data involves training a neural network and using it to make predictions, but this method treats test data as unknown, potentially leading to suboptimal predictions when test data is correlated with input data. To address this, a Bayesian neural network approach, called hNN, incorporates a hierarchical prior that allows for more accurate predictions by accounting for correlations between input and output data. Experimental results demonstrate hNN outperforms existing methods on actual stock market data.

In this study, local type spaces are explored within the context of continuous logic, with an emphasis on their connection to abelian groups, as established by the Pontryagin duality theorem. A specific type space, dubbed essential type space, is introduced to capture the relationship between type spaces and abelian groups, enabling us to identify every type space as a quotient of this essential type space. We also investigate the conditions under which essential type spaces exist, particularly in relation to density topological groups. A type space variant, called essentially separable type space, is introduced to examine groups with an essentially separable quotient. This study investigates the properties of these groups, demonstrating that a nontrivial compact topological group possesses an essentially separable group if and and only if its dual satisfies the $\sigma$-countable projective property. Additionally, it is shown that any type space can be represented as a direct sum of type spaces having compact underlying spaces.

This paper explores an innovative approach to tackling ethical concerns in machine learning by combining federated learning with differential privacy and fairness metrics. By leveraging federated learning, we address issues related to data security and bias mitigation, achieving this through biased model training and privacy-preserving noise injection. However, our research shows that standard noise injection methods can exacerbate existing model biases. Therefore, we propose the FairDPDP method, which integrates a novel noise injection strategy with a post-processing step to remove discrimination, thereby enhancing data privacy without increasing fairness. Our comprehensive evaluation of 10 fairness metrics, privacy measures, and classification accuracy across three datasets demonstrates the efficacy of our approach, which also outperforms existing methods, providing significant performance gains.

A simplified analysis is conducted to examine how a $Z'$ boson, which dark matter interacts with, affects searches for it, especially when considering the effect of a $X'$, with which both dark matter and standard matter interact. This interaction influences both the mass of dark matter and its distribution. However, current searches for dark matter do not account for how the $X'$ can alter relic abundance, which can significantly impact searches for it. For a wide range of masses, the effect of a $X'$ can make searches for dark matter less stringent. This can also influence the effect of other processes, such as annihilation to other particles, which can be impacted by the $X'$'s different behavior.

This research explores the application of deep unsupervised learning methods 
for wireless communication system design, using the K-means algorithm for 
comparative purposes, with the K-means approach involving the computation of 
exponential complexity based on the number of entries in the precoding matrix, 
whereas depth-wise separation in a three-layer convolutional neural network 
resulted in average MSE performance on par with K-means but at a reduced 
computational cost.

To assess the accuracy of beta decay strength distribution strength functions, we used a hybrid approach. We combined the experimental ground-state spins and spins from a joint angular momentum distribution with beta strength data from the Gaussian random matrix ensemble. We evaluated these strength functions in 14 nuclei within the $^{51}$V-$^{57}$Mn range, taking into account the different parent and daughter nucleus configurations and their impact on beta decay strength and nuclear energy level density. We also compared our findings to the literature and other theoretical models and assessed the impact of nuclear spin on beta decay strength.

We examine a model that combines dark matter with the scalar extension of the standard model, featuring the group symmetry $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R$, which we break down to $SU(2)_V$, while also introducing a $SO(4)\supset SU(2)_L \otimes SU(2)_R$ symmetry, which we break to $SU(2)_R$, and which allows for the existence of light singlets that interact with right-handed neutrinos. The scalar potential, which we analyze in detail, which includes the $SO(4)$ singlet, results in a non-trivial relationship between the dark matter relic density and the lepton flavour violating processes, which we relate to right-handed neutrino masses. The scalar sector, which we investigate in detail, which includes the $SU(2)_L$ and $SU(2)_R$ symmetries, which we break to $SU(2)_V$, which allows for the existence of heavy and light doublets that interact with each other, which results in a non-diagonal Higgs sector that allows for a relation between dark matter and right-handed neutrinos, which we relate to dark matter relic density and which we relate to scalar potential and which we relate to scalar potential and which we relate to scalar potential.

This paper presents an algorithm that integrates key elements of learning-based control techniques with optimal design strategies in order to minimize the impact of model uncertainty on control performance, particularly under limited data conditions. The learning-based control techniques leverage a model prediction error in the form of a cost function. To minimize the influence of uncertainty on performance, our algorithm introduces an automatic gain adjustment for this cost function, ensuring the most effective feedback linearization. To efficiently handle large-scale problems with limited data, we incorporate an iterative optimization strategy that gradually reduces the effect of uncertainty. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated through an acrobatic bicycle case study, where it is shown to achieve better performance with less data compared to traditional reinforcement learning methods.

We investigate the higher-spin symmetry in the context of Toda conformal field theories. This involves examining the higher-spin Ward identities and verifying their consistency with correlation functions obtained from the OPE expansion. The correlation functions' consistency necessitates a solution to the spin-three Ward identities, which we derive by showing their solution aligns with the higher-spin bootstrap equations. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the spin-three Ward identities impose constraints on the higher-spin theory, specifically fixing the relative normalization of the primary fields of the sl(n) algebra. These findings are also extended to the Polyakov-Maldacena-Zhytnik equations, illustrating their connection to the higher-spin symmetry.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of Relation Networks in enhancing the generation capabilities of Generative Adversarial Networks. By integrating Relation Networks into GANs, both one-to-one and one-to-many GAN architectures are proposed for image generation tasks. Experiments on the Celeba and LSUN-Church datasets reveal that the proposed architecture consistently outperforms conventional GANs. Notably, one-to-one GANs with the proposed architecture achieve higher PSNR and lower FID scores compared to StarGAN, while one-to-many GANs show superior performance over VAE and VAE-GAN baselines.

To enhance twin-field quantum key distribution, we introduce a novel method to establish a clear phase reference without relying on intense laser pulses. This method utilizes weak laser pulses from the signal channel and a simple mathematical model to establish the phase reference at the Bell state measurement node. We demonstrate through both theoretical analysis and a practical experiment that the new approach significantly lowers the Bell state measurement node's laser power requirement by more than 15 orders of magnitude compared to earlier methods. Furthermore, our implementation achieves a clear key rate distance relationship that surpasses the results of twin-field quantum key distribution systems that use a phase reference.

In this study, certain properties of Toeplitz operators are examined within the $p$-Bergman and $p$-Fock spaces of the unit disk, and those operators that are compact in these spaces are specifically identified, with some novel findings in this area presented.

This study introduces an efficient and straightforward technique for using active learning to automatically refine object detection models. Building upon the concept of pseudo 3D bounding boxes, we employ off-the-shelf 2D object detectors to assign initial bounding boxes to objects within the image, focusing the 3D object detection task on more critical areas. To minimize the number of samples requiring labels, we propose two efficient sampling methods. As a result, high-quality object detectors can be trained within a short time frame using active learning. Experiments confirm that active learning significantly enhances object detection performance, achieving results nearly equivalent to fully labeled datasets, while using less than 10% of the data. Furthermore, active learning provides robust object detection results, even when limited datasets are used.

The interstellar medium is comprised of ionized gas, neutral gas, and molecular gas, which is dispersed throughout the Galaxy. Observations of interstellar radio lines provide an opportunity to study the neutral and molecular phases of the IGM. A notable challenge in interpreting these observations arises from the effects of self-absorption. This phenomenon can distort spectral patterns, complicating the identification of associated ionized and molecular gas. This distortion may also be more pronounced in areas where regions of ionized and neutral gas are closely situated. A previous study found that ionized gas and molecular clouds are generally not adjacent in the Galactic plane. However, observations of the O-type stars indicate that regions of ionized and molecular gas can sometimes be very close together. A theoretical analysis of self-absorption in such areas is presented in this paper. Radio spectral line data from the VLA's Galactic hydrogen survey and Far-UV radiation from the GALEF mission have been used to examine the self-absorption of radio spectral lines in regions near O-type stars. A model of such regions was developed, and a comparison of the predicted and observed effects of self-absorption revealed that the effect is generally not significant. However, a notable increase in self-absorption was observed in regions near certain O-type stars. This result suggests that future radio line observations should account for the possibility of self-absorption, particularly in areas near O-type stars.

Convolutional networks and Transformers are powerful in solving image and language tasks, but their distinct approaches to inductive biases lead to significant performance gaps. In particular, Transformers are not naturally suited to handle spatial relationships, making it difficult to compare their and convolutional networks', in using identical datasets and models. To address this, researchers have turned to attention mechanisms to incorporate inductive biases into Transformers. A notable example is the development of Vision Transformers with Attention (ViTA), which incorporates additional biases to boost representation capabilities. ViTA, which uses two-dimensional attention mechanisms along with patch-masking, exhibits a striking similarity to convolutional networks, yet retains its flexibility in handling a variety of tasks. As a result, ViTA's performance is significantly improved and outperforms both convolutional networks and other vision attention mechanisms in multiple benchmarks.

This study develops a straightforward multivariate model for forecasting mortality rates, capable of incorporating multiple cohorts and time-varying mortality trends, which can be identified through factor analysis. By utilizing a new model type, a state-space multivariate non-stationary factor analysis model, the study demonstrates the potential for factor models with time-varying loadings to outperform the conventional CLM model in a long-term mortality forecasting study in New Zealand, with cohorts having been separated for more than half a century. Furthermore, the model's performance remains superior even when applied to cohorts with relatively short separation times. We also conduct an extensive out-of-sample analysis to determine the time series at which the new model exhibits superior forecasting capabilities.

A neural architecture search method named MoMoNeAS was proposed to reduce
interference within a shared weight space by employing multiple weight
initializations. This approach enabled the discovery of significantly improved
results in multiple natural language processing tasks, specifically
mathematical and logical reasoning. The performance of MoMoNeAS showed
considerable superiority over a control method, with results 26.5% and 21.6%
better on the REPLEX and LOGiSQA datasets respectively.

A time-series feature extraction library known as `theft` is introduced, designed to overcome the shortcomings of existing feature extraction packages, which often compromise on speed, transparency, and feature variety. By building on established feature extraction techniques, `theft` offers extensive feature coverage, full source code access, and high-performance optimization, making it suitable for analysis of large datasets.

We have demonstrated that geodesic completeness in the fundamental group is equivalent to geodesic completeness in the CAT(0) space and geodesic completeness in the quasi-isometry type. This group's geodesic completeness is further characterized as a combination of two properties: polynomial growth and geodesic completeness in its Cayley graph. When the group exhibits polynomial growth, its geodesic completeness is in turn determined by the absence of an infinite cyclic normal subgroup, which is in line with known results connecting CAT(0) geodesic completeness to torsion and growth in the case of cat(0) spaces. Additionally, we identify specific cases where the CAT(0) space is quasi-isometric to the geodesic completion of the Cayley graph of the group. These findings are based in part on prior work such as Rips' theorem, Ballmann-Lin, and Swarup' studies and contribute to resolving a problem posed by Swarup.

The shared task of GATEval has been established to provide language community members with a novel approach to translation quality evaluation, named gating metrics. This approach, which is highly automatable and suitable for large-scale machine translation quality assessment, offers an alternative to traditional methods. In our evaluation of the shared task participants, we mainly concentrated on two key aspects: the accuracy and generalizability of the translators and reviewers in predicting human translation quality. The accuracy assessment focused on comparing various neural-based quality assessment models, namely COMET, CHRF, and BLECOM, whereas generalizability analysis sought to determine which models performed best in predicting human translation quality on unseen data.

We introduce a comprehensive approach to dissect complex systems using a straightforward and mathematically robust framework. This method not only explains how different physical properties influence system behavior but also provides a clear and intuitive understanding of system dynamics. In particular, we demonstrate that the eigenvalue eigenvectors of a system represent the distinct wave patterns that make up the system's overall behavior. Moreover, we utilize a straightforward mathematical technique to analyze these wave patterns and identify the system's key characteristics. Through application of this method to various systems and comparison with numerical data, we confirm its effectiveness and reliability.

This study presents an innovative iterative magnitude pruning approach that achieves substantial efficiency improvements without compromising neural network performance. Developed in the context of visual tasks, the method proves effective in reducing both in-order and out-of-order computational overhead for neural networks. By applying it to standard ImageNet models, the proposed approach can decrease magnitude by 90% at various levels, resulting only in minimal accuracy decline for convolutional neural networks. Notably, it can convert a ResNet-50 architecture into an edge device-compatible model with 1.5 milliseconds latency. In addition, the method can be seamlessly integrated with graph neural networks, specifically for node classification tasks on CiteSeer, yielding impressive results with a 90% magnitude reduction. Adaptations for mixed hardware execution are also explored, including specialized hardware pruning tailored for pruning-aware out-of-order execution. Ultimately, the code for this proposed method is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/GeekMinds-Research/MAGPruning.

This study offers a unique, data-driven examination of lotteries from a buyer's perspective. The researchers found that super lotteries provide positive returns only when the jackpot reaches a certain high value, specifically between $660 million and $880 million. However, to purchase all tickets in these lotteries at an average price of face value would require the collective net worth of the top 10 million wealthiest individuals in the US. Meanwhile, more than $36 trillion is bet on lotteries annually worldwide. The findings indicate that lotteries attract buyers due to their ability to transform small amounts into substantial jackpots. Additionally, they reveal that a significant $22 billion in jackpot winnings go unclaimed annually.

The four-parameter O(N) coupled model, an alternative to the coupled fixed point theory, is a nontrivial model that can be studied through its large-charge expansion.  The model, with parameters alpha, beta, gamma, and delta, is analyzed using a coupled O(N) theory and the large-charge expansion to compute critical exponents.  The resulting critical exponents are in agreement with Monte-Carlo simulation results.

In nonuniformly strained environments, valley Hall transport is significantly altered due to the gradual change in valley-dependent band edges, causing particle trajectories to shift towards more favorable valleys.  To better understand this phenomenon, we apply kinetic theory and the Boltzmann transport equation, coupled with valley-dependent scattering processes, and investigate how sample width and boundary scattering affect valley Hall conductivity in WSe2.  Our research reveals that the magnitude of valley Hall conductivity is highly dependent on the valley relaxation time and temperature, and these effects can be quantified through our developed kinetic model.  By comparing valley Hall and electrical conductivities, we identify conditions under which the valley Hall effect is maximized, and discover that nonuniform strain variations can either facilitate or impede valley currents, respectively.

The domain adaptation task is typically addressed by averaging or fine-tuning the model on target domain data, but this often results in overfitting. Instead, the paper proposes the model soup (MS) approach, which fine-tunes a teacher model on the target domain, then combines multiple such models to create an ensemble that achieves both domain adaptation and overfitting prevention. By doing so, the MS approach yields superior results on multiple tasks, such as graph classification, which it compares favorably to other DA methods, as well as semi-supervised learning tasks, where it rivals existing state-of-the-art models.

We create a new, parametric version of t-SNE called PpSNE, which employs a localized probability distribution on spherical data, the Fisher-Rao, and has adjustable parameters $\sigma$ and $\nu$. The proposed distribution captures the characteristics of spherical data and adheres to an asymptotic property, and the associated pairwise probabilities are efficiently computed and optimized. The effectiveness of PpSNE is demonstrated through visualizations of 2D and 3D data, and the results indicate that it performs better than t-SNE, particularly in maintaining the integrity of the manifold structure of the dataset.

In our study, we have calculated the polaron's $Z$ factor, considering all relevant diagrams, for the weak to strong coupling regime. This was done using the self-consistent diagrammatic expansion method at zero temperature for the weak-coupling regime. We found that the $Z$ factor obtained from the full set of diagrams varies significantly from that derived from perturbation theory and perturbation theory relative to the band edge. Furthermore, we found that the polaron's mass calculated from the self-consistent diagrammatic expansion agrees well with that from perturbation theory relative to the band edge for weak interactions but diverges as the interaction strength increases. In addition, we found that the self-consistent diagrammatic expansion gradually converges towards the adiabatic atomic mass as the interaction strength increases from the weak-coupling regime to the strong-coupling regime where the polaron behaves like a bare atom.

For solving complex optimization problems, digital solutions are typically paired with heuristic methods. A newer digital approach can also tap into nature's potential by creating a hybrid digital-analog protocol. In this modified setup, we can mimic the dynamics of complex systems like the Fermi-Hubbard model using a trap of cold bosons. The digital component prepares an initial approximation, allowing it to be further refined through the analog simulation of evolution. Our investigation shows that even with limited precision, the digital approach can still recover highly accurate low-energy states of the Fermi-Hubbard model, facilitated by a simple correction process.

This research explores the use of isospectral matching polynomials for distinguishing between different graph structures, focusing on the sets of isospectral complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs. Similarly, sets of isospectral bipartite wheels and star-covered paths are identified and examined. In the process, the study reveals how the symmetry of a graph can lead to factorization in its matching polynomial. These findings suggest the development of new invariants for matching polynomials that can effectively rule out isospectral graphs.

The underlying mechanism driving the quantum asymptotics of Weyl multiplets under successive limit processes can be described using pseudo-Anosov elements, which serve as an asymptotic basis for the action of the Teichm\"uller isomorphism on wild geometric structures. This relationship gives rise to a family of convergent ideals within the center of a specific group, and through the study of the geometric structure's behavior under a group action, connections to wild geometric structures and 3-manifolds can be revealed, ultimately providing a framework for understanding semi-classical limits in 3d Chern-Simons theory.

This research investigates how the adoption of Scrum methods impacts project achievement in Scrum environments, even without face-to-face interactions. The study is carried out in an organizational context where participants interact via remote channels. To gather data, the study relies on interviews and online surveys. The results are analyzed to explore their implications and contribute to the existing body of knowledge. The findings are further discussed in relation to the existing literature and the study's limitations are also highlighted.

This paper delves into the concept of the "Gau--Wu determinant number," an extension of the "combinatorial determinant rank" concept, specifically tailored for matrix types like the arrow, block, and Hankel matrices. It explores the relationship between the Gau--Wu determinant number and linear dependencies among rows or columns in these matrices. Furthermore, the research focuses on calculating the Gau--Wu determinant number for arrow, block, and Hankel matrices under general conditions. Ultimately, the study derives the maximum possible values for the Gau--Wu determinant number across these matrices.

The proper decay lengths of beauty and charm particles, along with other backgrounds, have been analyzed using the ATLAS detector. By examining decays into specific final states, researchers found that the mean proper decay lengths of beauty baryons and charm baryons are 496 and 166 micrometers, respectively. These measurements are supported by existing data and open up new possibilities to study the internal structure of beauty particles.

This paper introduces a novel method of representing instances of object detection, segmentation, and objectification by utilizing points in a topological space. Each pixel is assigned a label indicating one of several color classes, and object instances are represented by points in a topological space, specifically the Nubra space, with N representing the number of color classes. Object instances that are distinct but connected in an image are mapped to the same class in the Nubra space by their corresponding points. Object instances' relationships and counts can be examined through the topological features created by the interaction of color classes through persistent homology, and these features can be captured in image descriptors for classification purposes. Our experiment demonstrates that our descriptor achieves state-of-the-art performance in classifications of object instances or their counts. Our work builds upon existing homological descriptors but differs by being applicable to object instances defined by bounding boxes or keypoint sets. Our method's versatility is demonstrated by its ability to be used for instances defined by pixel regions or keypoints, whether or not the objects are connected, and whether labeled by bounding boxes or segmentation masks. Our novel approach represents object instances by points in the Nubra space, enabling analysis of their relationships and counts through topological features generated by color class interactions.

This study investigates power control strategies within complex multi-user interference networks, focusing on binary power control and comparing its efficiency against optimal power control. An optimal distributed power control algorithm is proposed, offering a significant reduction in computational complexity. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that binary power control achieves at least 75% of the sum capacity possible in any given network. Moreover, we find that in large networks with numerous users, the sum capacity difference between binary and optimal power control approaches a 75% ratio, with optimal local updates converging towards binary power levels in large networks.

The vast amount of transaction data in today's complex business environment poses significant challenges for auditors to identify potential risks within their accounts. Traditional risk assessment methods are limited in their effectiveness, prompting researchers to explore new approaches that incorporate aspects of fuzzy logic and probabilistic reasoning. Building on this idea, we've developed a risk assessment model based on the Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence, which enables the representation of varying account risks. Our approach utilizes the combination of mass functions, corresponding to different transaction types of risk, to detect anomalies within an account by measuring discrepancies between the combined risk and individual transaction risks.

A new approach, Acceptance Rejection Stitching, has been devised for generating realizations of point process realizations, particularly Cramer processes, which includes important models like the Poisson Clustering process. The ARS method offers an alternative to traditional thinning methods, offering improved computational efficiency and the ability to scale with data size. The approach involves the use of thinning and rejection techniques, along with the computation of the cumulative distribution function of a characteristic function, which enables the rejection of points according to a uniform distribution. The performance of the ARS method has been evaluated against traditional methods, demonstrating significant speed improvements, particularly for processes with clustering behavior. The method allows for variable acceptance probabilities and optimizes computational efficiency by dividing the domain into regions. The performance of the ARS method is evaluated based on computational time and accuracy, with theoretical guarantees provided for accuracy. The results show significant speed improvements for processes with clustering behavior, achieving up to 10 times faster results than traditional methods. The method also provides accurate results with theoretical bounds on the probability of error. The implementation of the ARS method is available in the R package spatstat.

In this paper, we investigate the implications of Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) in the context of spacetime symmetries, specifically in deformed Galilean transformations, in a non-relativistic framework. Similar to the well-established GUP relativistic formulation, the GUP potential in our study retains a degree of flexibility in its general structure. As a result, the GUP potential that arises in the non-relativistic regime is found to be a linear combination of the GUP potentials from the traditional Lorentz transformations.

This research explores how dynamic task scheduling can be achieved in a multitasking environment, where processing power is not split into fixed portions but is instead allocated on a real-time basis in response to changing computational needs. While dynamic capabilities offer significant potential for reducing task execution times and improving system efficiency, we demonstrate that the optimal scheduling strategy depends on the rate of change in resource allocation. A novel, distributed dynamic scheduling approach is presented, which achieves these benefits while adapting to varying processing ratios and incorporating new methods for predicting and planning. Furthermore, we show that the optimal scheduling strategy is achieved when processing resources are allocated equally to each task.

This research explores controlled hopping of a single rigid link supported by a single spring on a soft surface. The objective is to analyze the impact of feedback control in accurately tracking desired periodic motion. The investigation uses computational simulations of a Rigid Link - Soft Ground model featuring a linear support spring. The results demonstrate that feedback control enables precise replication of nearly any open-loop periodic motion and minimizes deviations due to initial condition variations and external disturbances. Additionally, optimal open-loop periodic solutions were found by optimizing a cost function that accounts for trajectory deviations and control effort. The study's findings have significant implications for understanding simplified legged locomotion systems and biological jumping and running mechanisms.

We introduce an innovative approach to rapidly and reliably update large-scale IoT networks by utilizing simultaneous transmissions between firmware and individual devices. Our proposed solution, Firmware Over-The-Air Scaling Through Transmissions, enhances the speed at which a multitude of IoT devices can be updated without compromising on reliability. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our approach can achieve a substantial 10-fold increase in successful updates within a standard wireless network environment.

A novel method for studying the many-body localization (MBL) transition involves representing the eigenstates of disordered Hamiltonians using the eigenstates of a completely integrable model from the same space. This representation facilitates finding thermodynamic quantities and studying their nonergodic behavior, such as the variation in the fractal dimension associated with the self-energy across the MBL transition, and recovering MBL's sublinear magnetization in the thermodynamic limit. Furthermore, this method's effectiveness is demonstrated with warm atom experiments and atom trap Hamiltonians.

The Kalmann filter, a common solution for tracking multiple targets, faces a computational bottleneck due to a complex prediction step. To address this, the kBM-DP+ algorithm is proposed, using dynamic programming to break down the high-dimensional joint posterior into more manageable components. kBM-DP+ builds on a previous study, demonstrating the ability to handle non-Gaussian distributions without restricting target predictions to Gaussian priors. However, the study found that a more refined partitioning method led to significant performance improvements. kBM-DP-DP applies this partitioning technique to the prediction step, further breaking down the high-dimensional problem. kBM-DP-DP+ then uses particle methods to approximate an even more complex observation update step. In contrast to previous studies, kBM-DP-DP+ and kBM-DP-DP+ demonstrate computational efficiency comparable to the Kalman-BSF filter, with significantly reduced computational complexity. Additionally, kBM-DP-DP+ and kBM-DP-DP+ offer a notable improvement in estimation accuracy compared to the Kalman-BSF filter, with computational efficiency comparable to the Kalman-BSF filter.

Machine learning models, including those based on quantum algorithms, can be vulnerable to adversarial examples that cause them to make incorrect predictions by slightly altering the input data. In this context, the occurrence and characteristics of such attacks on quantum classifiers are explored through experiments on different quantum circuits, including variational classifiers and circuits with specific features like symmetry and feature mapping. The results indicate that adversarial attacks can significantly affect quantum classifier predictions, but this impact can be minimized in the case of quantum circuits with certain properties. However, it is also found that attacks may not always be feasible due to limitations imposed by quantum noise and error correction methods. Furthermore, attacks cannot always achieve optimal accuracy due to the complexity of the classification task. These insights can help guide efforts to create and evaluate quantum classifiers that are resistant to attacks.

The research involves analyzing the asymptotic behavior of volume normalized l-th Steklov eigenvalues in smoothly perturbed spherical domains, with a focus on determining specific mod-convergent sequences. Previous studies have been conducted for specific cases, such as by Bamberger and Ghosh in 2018 for spherically symmetric domains and Li in 2018 for non-negative homogeneous functions. This current research extends these results to the case where l is a square. For non-square l, it provides new results that demonstrate the volume normalized l-th Steklov eigenvalue converges to the sum of certain terms involving H_0, a specific function, and a coefficient, with the remainder of the sum being bounded by a certain expression. This research also extends Bamberger-Ghosh result to the case where l is not a square, showing the volume normalized l-th Steklov eigenvalue in the perturbed domain can be expressed as the sum of certain terms involving H_0, a specific function, and the remainder of the sum is bounded by a certain expression.

Process models serve as essential tools across various application domains, allowing for both formal mathematical representation and intuitive graphical depiction. Models primarily illustrate the sequence of tasks carried out, yet many recurrent tasks can be carried out in multiple valid orders. To effectively capture and analyze these complex execution sequences, we've developed new infix and postfix alignment techniques. These methods enable the representation of significant task groupings, either by always or conditionally order-ordering processes. These alignments are then applied to a wide range of real-world data sets from M2/M3/M4/M5, revealing that task groupings often occur more frequently than individual tasks. Furthermore, a frequency-weighted metric effectively captures recurring task patterns, offering valuable insights into business processes.

This study investigates the application of deep neural networks in creating a novel, accurate, and versatile radio propagation model, suitable for any urban area, by leveraging these neural networks' ability to learn complex patterns in data. A comprehensive dataset of 36 transmission locations and 41 reception points, accompanied by transmission data, was used to train and develop a deep convolutional neural network-based model, which accurately replicates propagation loss patterns across a detailed street map. A comparison with the conventional Cost231-H model reveals significant improvements in accuracy, with the deep neural network model achieving average absolute differences of 0.73 dB (test data) and 0.79 dB (training data) compared to 3.04 dB (test data) and 3.01 dB (training data). This research also introduces a universal training approach, enabling the model to be applied to any area without the need for additional training.

This study introduces a temporal planning system with validation integrated directly into its reasoning process. By doing so, it maximizes take advantage of validation's potential to enhance overall system performance. The integration is achieved through a novel model of temporal action logic (TAL) predicates, enabling the incorporation of validation algorithms in a type-safe manner. The practical implementation of this approach is demonstrated by the Temporal Factored Model Learning planner (TempoFol), which combines TAL with tailor-made, predicate-based tailer-generated constraints. As a result, it enables the creation of high-quality, learned constraints that can be used by the planner's decision procedure without compromising soundness. The proposed system, which features parallel processing of tree search and learning, was shown to significantly outperform its temporal factored $A^*$ planner, Folares, predecessor in terms of planning efficiency on a wide range of benchmark problems from the Strips-15 and Int-20 domains.

This study examines the impact of allocating generation capacities inefficiently on the overall system costs using the WPSM model, which models the power sector in Western Europe. The research utilizes the model's flexible temporal resolution to analyze the sensitivity of costs to additional information and additional information equivalents. The outcomes indicate that a misallocation of generation capacities due to insufficient temporal resolution results in substantially higher costs with finer models. Furthermore, relying on additional information equivalents to increase the model's temporal resolution can also lead to significantly inflated costs with more detailed models. The study's findings are general, as similar outcomes were obtained in multiple simulation scenarios.

We analyze one-dimensional periodic ionic Vlasov-Poisson models with multiple particle species, examining the behavior of solutions as the total mass in the system approaches zero, under Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions for the Poisson equations. These solutions, for any value of the mass parameter, converge to a unique solution of a Poisson equation with a parameter, representing the limiting behavior, in a linear fashion.

This paper outlines a search-based approach for software change tasks where required information is dispersed across a large code base. As software complexity increases, pinpointing relevant information becomes more challenging. Our approach builds upon a basic method of identifying suitable search terms through the analysis of text structures using TextRank and POSRank. To refine these terms, a topic-based algorithm called LTRE is employed, utilizing both the topic's word list and a similarity metric. The combination of these techniques has demonstrated a significant improvement in search precision and recall when compared to a baseline of keyword searches alone, with a notable increase in efficiency and reduced execution time.

A novel, ultrasound-assisted method to characterize the rheological properties of gels is introduced. The technique takes advantage of the fact that high-intensity ultrasound creates bubbles within a gel, inducing fluid movements and enabling visualization. By analyzing specific features of the resulting fluid dynamics in conjunction with low-intensity ultrasound, the model assumes that these patterns are linked to the loudness of the ultrasound, thus providing a way to characterize the mechanical properties of the gel without disturbing it. The approach was tested on a gel made of gelatin and gelatin with added clay particles, and the results showed that the characteristics of the dynamic patterns were consistent with expected variations in the gel's mechanical properties.
The research demonstrates how to apply the principles of mathematical induction to the Collatz conjecture.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence in diverse fields has led to a growing need for transparency in artificial neural networks. In this paper, we focus on enhancing the interpretability of machine learning models applied to text analysis, with a particular emphasis on document classification. By utilizing open-source tools, we demonstrate how to visualize the features that influence the network's decision-making process. Additionally, we explore the potential of open-source visualization tools to reveal how artificial neural networks process and interpret input data, and provide insights into the 'black box' by displaying the network's decision boundaries.

We have developed two novel extensions to the stable matchings framework:

- In the first model, each agent is associated with a positive real-valued utility function and receives ratings from their respective counterparts. We investigate two distinct scenarios where these ratings influence the matching process either through their average or through their respective individual utility functions.

- In the second model, we introduce discrete public ratings system where ratings can take values 0 or 1, which then influence the agents' utility functions accordingly.

We have made significant advancements in understanding these novel models:

- For the average rating scenario, we proved that when a worker has an unlimited market and a man has a market with a finite number of women, the man can achieve a better outcome than in the greedy stable matching.

- In the case where a woman has an unlimited market and a man has a market with a finite number of women, we found that greedy stable matching is optimal for the man, but we found that it is possible that no mechanism can achieve a better outcome than greedy stable matching for the woman, even when her market is much larger than his.

- In the case where public ratings system is used, we found that in some cases where a woman has an unlimited market and a man has a finite market, the average utility in the average rating mechanism is lower than in the case where the woman has no control over the system.

This paper presents a novel neural summary evaluation model, called SummScore, leveraging the capabilities of large pre-trained language models (PLMs) for automatic summary assessment. SummScore can be trained using self-supervised learning with just unlabeled data, and it can also be adapted to use weak labels for better performance. A key component of our approach is the evaluation metric called SummScore-Diversity, which outperforms existing metrics by more than 10% in correlation with human scoring, and also enables higher summary diversity compared to state-of-the-art methods.

To effectively process large-scale, multi-dimensional datasets, efficient data reduction techniques are essential for managing data overload and reducing storage requirements. While various methods have been developed to reduce dataset size, they often overlook the issue of introducing errors when data is reconstructed from reduced datasets. We examine how reducing the size of synthetic datasets affects their quality and the ability to accurately reconstruct sparse data. The size of the error introduced during reduction is quantified, and our findings indicate that the reducible sparsity of the data is directly proportional to the amount of cross-correlated information available. By using a system that generates independent, random measurements for each data variable, we can achieve a level of accuracy in which the majority of the dataset variables have their values exactly determined. The variability of the reconstruction error is dependent on the statistical properties of the reduction process, and this error is primarily caused by the reduction process itself, not the original measurement error. We also investigate the effect of original dataset error on dataset reduction.

This research presents a novel, robust end-to-end object detection system called BEVfusion, which utilizes data from both cameras and LiDAR to make objects visible in 2D image spaces visible in the 3d bird's eye view (BEV) space. The proposed system enhances performance by breaking down complex predictions into simpler, data-driven sub-tasks. A contrastive learning framework is introduced to accurately sync features extracted from cameras and LiDAR, with results demonstrating that the model surpasses traditional fusion methods by 0.9 AP, while also demonstrating improved resilience in the event of LiDAR malfunctions by 2.8 AP.

We introduce a novel understanding of turbulent fluid dissipation that integrates both deterministic and stochastic Navier-Stokes equations. The traditional Navier-Stokes equation, which is a component of our discussion, is a fundamental aspect of fluid dynamics, but we also discuss turbulent dissipation in the context of fluid dynamics. The introduction of fluctuating hydrodynamics (FHE) in 2D and 3D reveals that the FHE equation, which includes a stochastic force, can accurately predict and reproduce the intensity of turbulence in both fully developed turbulent flows and transient states. The forces involved in turbulence are known as Reynolds stresses, which are a linear function of the fluid's velocity gradient and the intensity of turbulent fluctuations. The forces are balanced by a modified viscosity term, which is called turbulent viscosity. The turbulent dissipation rate is found to be a combination of fluid and turbulent viscosity, which is called the turbulent dissipation rate. The turbulent dissipation rate is a unique quantity that is independent of fluid properties and is a function of the Reynolds number and other parameters. The introduction of stochastic calculus in fluid dynamics provides a theoretical basis for the relationship between turbulence and dissipation. The Feynman-Kac theorem and the Feynman-Kac formula are used to establish the connection between turbulent dissipation and Brownian motion. The turbulent dissipation rate is a unique quantity that is a function of the turbulent dissipation rate and the turbulent dissipation rate. We demonstrate an experimental approach for measuring thermal patterns within a thermal fluid, with applications in thermal imaging, flow visualization, and heat management systems. This approach leverages the thermal gradient-induced refractive index in the fluid, which distorts a laser beam through complex, thermally-induced refraction phenomena. By analyzing these patterns, real-time temperature maps can be determined, although the refractive index and temperature are linked, making the mapping process non-trivial. Our experiment involves heating a thin layer of fluid using a heated object, which we analyze with a analysis algorithm based on the assumption that the thermal pattern within the fluid is linked to the observed laser diffraction pattern. Our experimental results show a high degree of accuracy between the actual and estimated temperature patterns.

The design repository harnessing experience from similar projects is an essential tool for guiding design decisions. By analyzing the layout of prior designs, this guide can be created, yet current approaches for extracting design insights suffer from inconsistent outcomes and fail to apply across different projects. By applying automatic decoding techniques and a more robust filtering process, we enhance the stability and applicability of extracted design insights, leading to a significant improvement in evaluation metrics. We conduct thorough evaluation in an academic and human setting, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which yields human-comparable performance in extracting similar designs and exceptional success in applications of automatic guidance. The results of our work have been publicly released to facilitate future investigations.

The proliferation of IoT devices has led to a significant increase in both the speed and quantity of data generated, posing significant challenges for managing and processing this data. While some solutions rely on a distributed architecture, they often neglect the complexities inherent in data streams, rendering them ineffective. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel data stream processing system called H-STREAM, which is capable of handling high-speed and high-volume data streams on a cost-effective single-board computer. H-STREAM employs a sophisticated data stream clustering technique based on the DBSCAN algorithm, which is specifically tailored for rotating calipers and incorporates optimizations such as vectorization, the elimination of redundant distance calculations, and the reduction of memory access. These enhancements allow H-STREAM to achieve improved performance, which is validated by experimental results. H-STREAM outperforms existing systems by a substantial margin in terms of speed and supports a larger number of data sources, all while being deployable on low-cost hardware.

A novel method of calculating the cross-section for vector-like quark pair and single production has been developed. This innovative approach involves separately computing the cross-sections of resonant and non-resonant diagrams, and then merging them using a smooth transition. An approach utilizing a complex mass parameter was found to effectively combine the cross-sections for both quark pair and single production. As a result, no substantial gaps in naturalness appear in the mass spectra of vector-like quarks. The new formula is highly accurate, and it correctly accounts for the influence of non-resonant diagrams on cross-section estimations that are typically based on a cascade decay path. Moreover, the formula is robust and it remains valid even in scenarios where the mass difference between the vector-like quark and its partner is relatively small, and up to the TeV energy range in single production analyses.

This research addresses the significant challenge of generating SPARQL queries, which can automatically transform natural language statements into executable SPARQL queries. Given a knowledge graph and natural language statement, the associated generated query retrieves relevant entities from the graph. Existing approaches, including those based on encoder-decoder architectures, achieve reasonable results but fall short in complex tasks. This paper introduces SPARQL-GIN, which surpasses existing encoder-decoder architectures. The proposed model employs a graph isomorphism network to learn entity relationships and an attention-based decoder to learn query structure. Additionally, the inclusion of a copy mechanism significantly enhances performance by allowing the model to copy entities from the knowledge graph. SPARQL-GIN outperformed encoder-decoder architectures in experiments, achieving an improvement of 15% in F1 score. The code for SPARQL-GIN is available at https://github.com/SpaRQL-GIN/SPARQL-GIN.

Our research has centered on the publication venues of Computer Science sub-fields, which exhibit distinct temporal characteristics. By examining these venues over a 30-year period, we aimed to gain insights into the evolving landscape of CS research. To achieve this, we employed a venue evolution model that tracks the lifespan and shifting sub-field associations of each venue. The inherent complexity of this problem made it a suitable candidate for applying complex analysis and machine learning techniques. The innovative approaches we've developed in this field have not only shed light on the temporal dynamics of CS sub-fields but also paved the way for analyzing the life cycles of individual publications and publication venues.

Ensuring the reliability of control systems that use neural networks is crucial, 
especially with the development of complex systems in the real world.  In a recent
study, mathematical methods for assessing neural network resilience in control 
systems are evaluated and potential connections to computer vision and machine 
learning advancements that could improve this process are identified and explored.
Key network design and training strategies that could support verification 
effort are analyzed in detail.  In addition, network performance metrics that 
prioritize resilience are proposed and the challenges of balancing accuracy and 
safety are discussed.  Finally, specific verification methods that are currently 
being developed for use in the control systems community are outlined along with 
their respective strengths and weaknesses.

Functorial clustering schemes are utilized to transform finite metric spaces into posets, extending previous applications. However, the limitation of single-linkage clustering being applicable only to complete metric spaces necessitated an exploration of its defects when spaces are non-complete. Posets constructed from single-linkage clustering exhibit strong structural properties and our investigation focuses on understanding the 'disagreement' caused by applying this scheme to non-metric spaces. Building upon earlier work, we demonstrate that single-linkage clustering is a specific instance of a more general, functorial approach known as 2-cosheafy clustering. Furthermore, utilizing the notion of 'glueing errors' from 2-cosheaf theory, we are able to characterize the 'defects' of single-linkage clustering through a functor called linkage curvature. This new invariant quantifies the degree to which spaces deviate from being metric and provides valuable insights into the geometric implications of applying single-linkage clustering to non-metric spaces.

Real-world applications of tensor completion, such as monitoring satellite devices, analyzing brain activity, and monitoring motion, are heavily impacted by movement. Traditional streaming algorithms, tailored for static data, often underperform in scenarios involving motion. To rectify this, a new family of algorithms, LMAVT, has been developed, leveraging the characteristics of moving data, and accommodating the potential errors caused by motion. By decomposing the video into smaller, manageable parts and applying a time-constrained learning method, LMAVT is effective for processing both still and moving data. Additionally, a version of LMAVT, called TLMAVT, incorporates the most recent data to efficiently handle extremely long videos. Numerical results indicate that LMAVT outperforms other algorithms in monitoring motion, while TLMAVT enables the use of LMAVT on massive datasets, such as long satellite monitoring and fMRI analysis.

This study categorizes certain complex Nichols algebras associated with specific symmetries found in classical Weyl groups as either boundless or confined materials. A preliminary assessment of these restricted materials reveals the underlying algebraic composition of self-contained Hopf subalgebras comprising the allowed components.

Researchers investigated the inertial wave turbulence in their research, which has been experimentally verified to comply with the $k^{-7/3}$ spectrum first predicted analytically by Godeferd and Moisy. They examined the turbulent dynamics of weakly damped inertial waves generated through beta-effect modulated forcing, an approach previously explored in laboratory settings. By analyzing the outcomes from their research, which involved forcing at different rotation rates, they were able to observe the predicted $k^{-7/3}$ spectrum and its characteristics near the stability limit. Furthermore, they were able to track the behavior of the predicted spectral energy maximum as rotation was varied, which showcased the unique features of the two-dimensional turbulent dynamics governed by the Coriolis force, particularly near the stability limit of the forcing.

We and others have recently found that if a graph undergoes an iterative normalization process, where connected vertices are replaced with single nodes, it is equivalent to solving the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem in the graph. This happens because the graph structure changes in a specific way under certain conditions. A numerical study has been conducted to analyze how the solution changes over time and if the estimated solution is close to the true one, even after many iterations. A further investigation has been done to see if the expected structure is observed in more complex problems and whether it is possible to predict fast convergence based on specific graph characteristics. A proposed modification to the standard problem, which involves requiring certain pairs of vertices to be at a minimum distance apart, is formulated and studied under an iterative process to determine its feasibility and convergence. A specific case of this modified problem, which involves a minimum distance of 2, is observed to be the same as a well-known problem in network analysis, which pairs vertices in a graph in a specific way. A theoretical analysis has been conducted to see if the number of steps needed for the structure to change in a specific way is at most quadratic, which is at most the square root of the number of vertices in the graph. A theoretical analysis has been conducted to see if the expected minimum convergence rate is at least a certain number, which is at least a specific number divided by the square of the number of vertices in the graph.
