A new task called Perpetual View Generation is proposed, which is a more difficult
extension of the traditional view generation task due to its significantly larger
number of output images and diverse starting points. This task is particularly
challenging as it requires the model to be able to recall a vast number of detailed
object views and generate corresponding images from novel camera angles. We introduce
two approaches to address these requirements: Multi-step View Generation using Strong
Priors and latent space exploration, and an innovative technique for pinpointing
specific feature directions within the latent space to generate highly accurate views.
Extensive testing on a well-established dataset has shown that our proposed method outperforms
other techniques and has yielded promising results in real-world applications involving
the creation of novel images from limited available data.

The complexity of model predictive control (MPC) in large networks can be reduced through effective techniques that exploit networked interconnections. Building upon recent research that applied the Koopman operator to linear MPC, this paper presents a new method that combines Koopman operator theory with task decomposition. This approach divides the control problem into smaller sub-problems, models each independently, and re-integrates them to achieve the desired outcome. A simulation of a DC microgrid with renewable energy sources and smart loads demonstrates the proposed method's effectiveness in efficiently managing complex network controls.

When a thin liquid film forms on the surface of a cylinder and is influenced by gravity, a series of developing bubbles or drops form on its surface. These develop through a series of instabilities, specifically a primary instability that causes periodic thickening and secondary instabilities that further thicken the liquid. This primary instability occurs at different rates depending on whether the fibre is smooth or rough. When the fibre is smooth, the primary instability always occurs, but when the fibre is rough, the primary instability occurs at higher speeds and is controlled by the speed of the surrounding liquid. This change in behavior can be used to control the formation of liquids on the surface of a cylinder.

We investigate the geometric structure of compressible perfect fluid dynamics in Lagrangian coordinates, where a coordinate transformation is applied to a reference fluid configuration metric. Our approach employs an extended Euler阿尔-Guderman metric in three-dimensional Lagrangian coordinates, which incorporates the complexities of Lagrangian coordinates and the variability of metric coefficients. Our analysis reveals that in three-dimensional Lagrangian coordinates, the Euler阿尔-Guderman metric exhibits a distinct geometric structure, significantly differing from its Eulerian coordinates counterpart. Furthermore, by introducing a coordinate transformation, we demonstrate that the Euler阿尔-Guderman metric in three-dimensional Lagrangian coordinates can be reduced to a Riemannian metric under the condition that fluid elements do not intersect, whereas under general conditions, it remains in the form of bi-metric geometry.

Scoliosis, a condition characterized by an irregular curvature of the spine, is often associated with an uneven distribution of spinous process angles. However, measuring the spine in patients with scoliosis can be challenging. A novel robotic ultrasound system has been developed to address this challenge, but the reliability of its measurements has not been thoroughly investigated. In a study involving 10 scoliosis patients, the inter- and intra-examiner reliability of spinous process angle measurements were assessed. A total of 14 experienced examiners performed the measurements twice, with the study focusing on two different measurements. On average, 10 different examiners performed the measurements twice, with the study focusing on two different measurements. The results showed that the robotic ultrasound system had good to excellent inter- and intra-examiner reliability for spinous process angle measurements in scoliosis patients.

Project planning and management heavily rely on predicting task durations, 
which is typically a complex process with a wide range of possible outcomes.
This complexity is often overlooked, however, as project managers usually work 
with singular, deterministic time estimates, which can lead to inaccurate results.
This paper introduces an advanced duration modeling technique that generates 
probability distributions rather than a single value for task durations.
This approach allows project managers to visualize and quantify the 
uncertainty surrounding task completion times.
The proposed method integrates task descriptions with keywords that inform 
software agents about the expected duration distribution of each task.
This results in a more accurate and reliable estimation of task durations.
The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a practical case study of 
software development using agile methodology.

This paper presents the outcome of the OSU team's participation in SemEval-2020 Task 7, 
where the objective was to identify and classify hate speech in social media posts.
We conducted an experiment to classify hate speech in 4 languages: English, Spanish, Arabic and Russian.
Our team initially explored three approaches: utilizing pre-trained language models and combining them with BERT.
Our analysis revealed that fine-tuning BERT yielded the most successful results.
We achieved the best outcome in the English dataset, and were ranked second in the Spanish dataset, 
with one gold standard annotation removed by the organizers.

A novel hierarchical structure is presented for the unsupervised learning of representations in complex data sets. This framework combines two key components: a network designed to isolate and remove subtle information from learned representations, and a auxiliary module that ensures the extracted information maximally contributes to predicting outcomes. This subgoal module acts as a constraint on the representation learning process, thereby preventing the over-extraction of excessive details. To address the over-learned subnetworks that attempt to capture excessive information, our approach includes an unmixing step that rectifies over-extraction by fusing over-extracted and under-extracted information. This network structure is highly versatile, allowing it to be easily adapted to various tasks and domains. This adaptation includes applications in unsupervised image denoising, multi-modal learning, and learning from noisy labels. Notably, our approach demonstrates strong performance in improving model robustness under noisy labels and achieves superior denoising and multi-modal learning results.

Document analysis is a difficult task to find the right dataset for. Although there are numerous datasets available for historical documents, they are not all relevant. A problem arises when researchers have to sift through numerous datasets to find the one that fits their specific analysis needs. To address this issue, we have developed a new dataset meta-database that provides a comprehensive collection of information on historical document datasets, making it easier for researchers to find the right dataset for their specific analysis requirements. By incorporating a user-friendly search interface and rich search capabilities, the dataset meta-database will streamline the process of locating the right dataset for a particular research project.

This study proposes a solution to enhance the trajectory tracking precision of flexible industrial robots by implementing model predictive control strategies. Initially, we leverage a dynamic model of the robot, incorporating both rigid and flexible components, to forecast the robot's movement and final state. Subsequently, we utilize this predictive capability within the framework of a model predictive control algorithm designed to optimize trajectory tracking accuracy. Since the predictive tracking error is characterized by a complex, non-linear nature, we apply piece-wise linear approximation techniques through a method of sequential linearization. Following this, we transform the trajectory tracking accuracy optimization problem into a sequence of simpler quadratic programming problems that can be efficiently solved using the iterative reweighted least squares algorithm. The efficacy of our proposed control strategy is validated using data from the PUMA 560 robot, demonstrating significant improvement in trajectory tracking accuracy.

The prevalence of chronic health issues linked to myocardial infarction, found in a person's electronic health record, is typically used to gauge their long-term health status. However, these data can be influenced by sex and other socio-demographic characteristics, which this study aims to clarify. Utilizing electronic health records from over 1.5 million people in England between 2013 and 2018, the research examines how chronic health conditions affect people of different sexes and backgrounds. The results indicate distinct patterns in chronic health prevalence among men and women, as well as across various ethnic groups, which are not solely explained by migration patterns, age, or calendar year. Moreover, significant disparities in chronic health prevalence are observed between groups, and these differences are not entirely attributed to variations in migration patterns, calendar year, or sex. Ultimately, collecting and analyzing sex and ethnic-specific chronic health data are essential for a thorough understanding of long-term health status and the design of targeted prevention and management programs.

Our research explores a customized approach to Becke's method for computing local exchange-correlation energy, designed to facilitate faster computation across an infinite range of values for integrals like those involving electronic continuum. The custom method utilizes a compact representation of Gaussian density functions and demonstrates significant convergence acceleration in Variational Monte Carlo integration across one and three dimensions.

The Metric Dimension problem parameterized by multiple graph parameters has seen considerable research, with the problem being both non-FPT and not hard to prove linear time lower bounds when using certain parameters, according to recent studies.  A recently identified problem is the wide disparity in the level of APX-optimality among different graph parameters.  We investigate the possibility of the local density of a graph being used to distinguish the level of APX-difficulty, with the surprising finding that the level of APX-difficulty within the family of trees is independent of local density.  We present two tree-like graph families where the Metric Dimension problem can be solved in polynomial time and another where it cannot be approximated within a certain ratio by considering the presence of cliques in the parameters.  Moreover, we observe that there is a sudden change occurring when local density reaches 3, with the Metric Dimension problem becoming significantly more difficult as a result.

For any partially ordered set (poset) $P$, Scott gave a partial order for the power set of $P$ (containing finite elements) by restricting the upper power set order (which orders based on inclusion). In contrast, three different partial orders exist on directed spaces equipped with Scott topology, specifically upper, lower, and convex power spaces, all of which utilize lower and upper approximation operators to approximate the non-finite power set elements. These directed space power set orders differ significantly from those power set orders used in dcpos (which have the Scott topology).

In lower-tropospheric regions, high cloud cover is associated with significant radiative heating. Research indicates that in hothouse climates characterized by two stable states, lower-tropospheric heating plays a crucial role in driving cloud patterns and precipitation changes, ultimately contributing to the transition between these states, whereas conventional greenhouse models lacking such conditions cannot produce similar behavioral complexities, underscoring the importance of lower-tropospheric heating in inducing non-linear climate dynamics and the potential for hysteresis in climate transitions.

The de Rham complex of differential forms on a 2D Poisson manifold can be described by a higher-spin extension of Yang-Mills theory with action S_VV given by the integral of the higher-spin de Rham complex cohomology representative. This theory includes a derivation D of the de Rham complex and has additional symmetry. When the underlying Poisson manifold has a commutative algebra of differential forms, we derive expressions for the anomaly and quantum action. These expressions facilitate identification of the quantum-de Rham complex.

A deep neural network training process is severely hindered by incorrect labels. The existing methods designed to correct these inaccuracies are mostly based on pre-existing knowledge. In this study, we present the first fully adaptive solution, using Bayesian statistics and a label refurbishment approach guided by Bayesian reasoning. This novel method, known as BLRM, allows for the automatic identification of noisy training samples without external input. A comprehensive evaluation of BLRM is conducted using a wide range of datasets, including the MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and SIFT-1k datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that BLRM consistently enhances the performance of the underlying deep neural networks in noisy environments, with varying degrees of contamination across these datasets.

We examine the infinite dimensional case of interpolation through a nondegenerate regular simplex in the unit cube space, having $n+1$ nodes in $Q_{n}$ for any $n$. Research by V. A. Savchuk and others established that such simplexes can approximate the set of all functions in $Q_{n}$, but the measure of error decreases at a rate that depends on the number of $n$'s. In contrast, our work shows that a specific condition, $n+1 \geq 2d$, is necessary and sufficient to achieve a decrease rate that depends on $d$. Additionally, our analysis leads to a new, more accurate estimate for Lebesgue constants in the context of Lebesgue polynomials at $n$ nodes, with this condition also being the benchmark for our findings.

The articles by K. Allanson and A. So and the K. Allanson, A. So, and J. Zhang papers
investigate random walk models where the underlying underlying space R is not bounded.
Our analysis centers on the one-dimensional case where we calculate the characteristic polynomial
of the transition probability matrix P(h)(k) for the correlated random walk and R with arbitrary correlation coefficient rho.
Our solution is more general than those in the existing literature as it assumes no restriction on rho being non-negative or correlation being more than 0.5.
Our approach involves using the Fourier transform to obtain a closed form for the probability mass function and the latter method leads to the derivation of the characteristic polynomial for the correlated random walk.

Automated theorem provers for termination can struggle with complex programs like interpreters and bootstrappers that utilize a clock to count steps, often leading to convoluted proof methods. To address this issue, we propose a streamlined approach for termination proofs that utilizes simplified, de-clocked versions of the original programs. This method leverages coupled mutual transformations, effectively proving the synchronized execution of the de-clocked and clocked programs, ultimately facilitating simpler termination arguments. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach by implementing a mutual inductive definition in Isabelle/HOL, validated through concrete examples.

The hairpin packet, an essential building block in wall-bounded turbulence, has been the focus of numerous studies. Various theories have been proposed to explain its structure and behavior. This work provides an in-depth analysis of the evolution of the hairpin packet through a simulation, aiming to clarify its structure and dynamics. The simulation results reveal that the connection between wall turbulence elements and new structures involves a process rather than a sudden transformation. It has been observed that the hairpin packet's shape changes over time, contradicting established models. Furthermore, the 3D nature of the vortex ring and the role of turbulence elements in new structure formation have been highlighted. The simultaneous development of streamwise vortices and new packets was shown, contrasting previous assumptions. This research contributes to understanding the complex interactions in wall turbulence and identifying patterns in new structure formation.

A particular instance of the $O(3)$ baby Skyrme model, featuring cubic and quartic terms, has been re-engineered to include gauge fields. The resulting Lagrangian density, when not influenced by gauge fields, reduces to the established Skyrme Lagrangian. Three distinct soliton profiles described in polar coordinates have been identified: those profile shapes match those in the original Skyrme model. By applying a specific gauge, soliton energies can be calculated and shown to be equivalent to the energies in the Skrrme model. The inclusion of gauge fields' effect on soliton behavior has also been investigated.

We analyze the Weyl semimetal behavior in a lattice model where mass terms are influenced by vector-like Minkowski spacetime coordinates. By removing crystal symmetry in the Minkowski mass matrix, we find that the lattice model's behavior changes, eliminating the infinite phase transitions and establishing a single phase, consistent with the continuum limit. However, reintroducing crystal symmetry restores diverse phase transitions, where a phase transition may occur when the crystal symmetry breaks at a certain threshold of the Minkowski coordinate mass. This situation parallels the presence of magnetic monopoles in a free theory of Quantum Electrodynamics, where magnetic monopoles can be viewed as the lattice's remnant of crystal symmetry.

The occurrence of Fano resonance in coupled optical nanoantennas is heavily influenced by their respective spectral modes. We have demonstrated through numerical and analytical research that the spectral locations of both dark and bright resonances, as well as their contrast, can be independently adjusted by manipulating the energy exchange between coupled modes. The principle of the concept is shown through an example of L-shaped plasmonic nanoantennas, and the research has significant implications for optical resonance applications.

In the investigation of the mechanical properties of glass, both in its static and dynamic forms, we've found that sudden bursts of plastic deformation, known as avalanches, can have a substantial impact. These avalanches, resulting from the cascading movements of disordered materials, are primarily governed by the lengths of these plastic events. Notably, our research reveals that these bursts significantly influence the overall mechanical response, especially in older and less elastic samples. The incorporation of such plastic plasticity into existing models of elastic materials, which typically ignore these bursts, may lead to inaccurate representations of the mechanical behavior. To better comprehend this phenomenon and its implications, we propose the development of continuum theories that account for both elastic properties and plastic events, which are essential in understanding the mechanical properties of older and less elastic amorphous materials.

Using ab initio methods and density functional theory, researchers investigated the effect of Mn decoration on the electronic properties of silicene with a graphene-like honeycomb structure. They found that the parameter of Hubbard interaction on Mn-decorated silicene is significantly higher than that of pure silicene depending on the specific Mn placement. It was also observed through direct simulation of the many-body Hamiltonian that the majority of correlation-induced spin polarization localizes on the decorated Mn sites, resulting in a silicene band structure that closely resembles that of a metal. Notably, the spin polarization exhibits a dependence on Mn decoration concentration, showing a direct proportionality in the range of low to intermediate levels of concentration before saturation occurs.

A multi-wavelength study of Sgr A East, a supernova shell in the Galactic plane, has provided a detailed analysis. The supernova, associated with the Crab nebula, is at a distance of about 8 kiloparsecs from the centre of the Galaxy. A previous study in 1975 used radio observations to locate Sgr A East in the Galactic plane. A new, comprehensive study combines the results from various telescopes to provide a comprehensive picture of Sgr A East. A 12 GHz radio observation made with the VLA in 1975 revealed a bright radio source at 2.1 arcseconds from the centre of Sgr A East. To examine the impact of class imbalance on the performance and calibration of algorithms, we conducted a systematic study on the imbalance metric and its correlation with the 0-one error calibration. The chosen metric, $\gamma$, represents the ratio of the minority class sample count to the majority class sample count. Experiments were performed on the 0-one error of 2 algorithms from different families, specifically the 1-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), and a neural network (NN) trained with binary cross-entropy and temperature scaling. To simulate class imbalance, we modified the sampling method to over-sample minority classes and under-sample the majority classes. To replicate the class imbalance impact on KNN and SVM, we compared their 0-one error on imbalanced datasets to the 0-one error of minority-class samples in balanced datasets. Conversely, to simulate class imbalance impact on NN, we compared the 0-one error of NN on imbalanced datasets to the 0-one error of NNN samples. Our research focused on 3 classification tasks: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. To replicate the class imbalance impact on various tasks, we used the class imbalance rates found in real-world datasets. Our results indicate that, for nearest-neighbor and SVM-based classifiers, performance degradation is directly linked to the class imbalance rate. Conversely, for neural networks, performance degradation is not affected by class imbalance rate.

This research explores the spread of COVID-19-related news on local social media, focusing on online platforms within the US, particularly investigating online interactions and local events. By using search engine data and online activity metrics, we mapped and analyzed content, geographic distribution, timing, and temporal patterns of COVID-19 coverage. Our analysis revealed a strong link between local news on social media and online events, but not timing. By combining these insights, we provide an in-depth understanding of COVID-19's local impact. Our study's data and analysis are publicly available, allowing for further local event mapping. Our findings highlight the value of local coverage and its potential to support public health.

The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is a widely used technique in astrophysics to optimize the computational cost of gravitational calculations, which typically scale with the square of the number of particles ($N^2$). By partitioning particles into hierarchical cells, FMM approximates distant particle groups as single entities to reduce the complexity of interactions. Although FMM has been successfully applied to electromagnetic simulations, its implementation for gravity often omits certain methodological details, particularly when dealing with the translation and factorization of particle interactions. In this research, the translation coefficients and an expansion order optimization strategy are described in the context of a Newtonian gravitational potential, allowing for an analytical expansion up to the quadrupole term using an adapted version of spherical harmonic translation coefficients for electromagnetic simulations. Furthermore, this work demonstrates an optimization approach to determine optimal expansion orders based on the distance between particle cells and the radius of the smaller cell, which, when tested on the 'icecube' galaxy, shows significant computational savings.

The HERMES experiment collected data for its measurement of the double spin asymmetry in elastic electron-proton scattering, using a polarized hydrogen target and integrating over a range of momentum transfers. Data collection involved $2.15 \times 10^{11}$ photons exchanged, with HERMES recording both right- and left-handed helicity data and integrating over the range of momentum transfers from 0.25 to 3.04 $Gev^2$. The resulting elastic electron-proton data shows the contribution of the GM1 form factor, with results consistent with those of the HERMES experiment's inclusive measurement, and with previous experiments' measurements of the proton GM1 form factor, with data collected from both right- and left-handed helicity data.

The augmented policy cloning method allows for the efficient learning of high-dimensional control tasks by augmenting state variables with policy outputs. This semi-supervised approach, requiring minimal data, enables student policies to accurately replicate expert behavior. Our focus lies in understanding the underlying reasons for the success of this method, which can be examined from the perspective of both the learning algorithm and the particular control problems in question. Through theoretical and numerical analyses, we examine how such issues can be addressed by considering the joint state-policy space. Our findings suggest that augmented policy cloning can be viewed as a special instance of a more widely applicable unsupervised pre-training method. This technique has been successfully applied to complex control tasks such as dexterous robot arm manipulation.

A novel search for heavy scalar or pseudoscalar resonations decaying into two photons is introduced. This search utilizes the dominant production mechanism of the Higgs boson, specifically through the interaction of the heavy scalar S or pseudoscalar A with the Higgs boson H, in the context of the effective field theory framework. The Higgs boson in this search is assumed to decay into two photons, as detected in the 13 TeV proton-proton collisions data collected by the CMS experiment, amounting to 138 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity. Two significant findings were made: a lack of a signal in the search for the production of heavy scalar S with masses between 500-1500 GeV and neutral pseudoscript A with masses between 400-1500 GeV, both at a 95% confidence level. Furthermore, the search's sensitivity in terms of the production cross-section times the branching ratio is established, and the potential for future searches is outlined.

The nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) community is currently exploring quantum computing, with dynamic decoupling techniques being a focal point.  However, another application, the resonant spin maser, is also leveraging dynamic decoupling.  While some maser systems use simple pulse sequences, others employ digital signal processing to optimize frequency detection.  A dynamic decoupling scheme was designed to be compatible with both digital signal processing and analog detection, allowing for the detection of narrow frequency peaks in a maser system.  Using a $^{171}$Yb maser with 12 qubits, experimental results were found to be in line with theoretical models, and it was observed that digital signal processing could effectively narrow frequency peaks while masmer systems without digital signal processing could experience broader linewidths due to noise.  These findings are significant for maser systems that aim to merge quantum information processing and signal processing.

This article establishes a common framework for analyzing hypergeometric groups in connection with the symmetries of K3 surfaces, drawing on the rationale initially set forth by C. Voisin in \cite{Voi}, and we provide a concrete example to illustrate the concept.

A new, "hidden sector" neutralino is theorized to mix with neutralinos from the visible sector, providing an alternative explanation for dark matter's abundance in the universe. This novel concept predicts that visible sector neutralinos can decay into hidden sector neutralinos and high-energy gamma rays, observable as gamma ray emissions from dark matter within galactic and extragalactic regions. Nevertheless, these gamma ray emissions may be obscured by background radiation from cosmic sources, particularly pi-zero mesons within galactic regions. Additionally, point-like gamma ray emissions from individual dark matter cosmic sources may be hidden by contributions from their surrounding halos, exemplified by the Sun and the center of the galaxy. This study proposes an innovative method to eliminate the background influence of cosmic halos, allowing for the detection of cosmic sources that emit gamma ray emissions due to dark matter annihilations. Furthermore, a gamma ray spectrum analysis of the Sun is presented, suggesting that the dark matter annihilation signal may be distinguishable from surrounding contributions.

We propose a novel, dynamic approach to computing a graph's genus, and present an implementation in the system 'gencalc'. Our method involves gradually increasing the graph's complexity by adding edges, and it relies on a fundamental theorem that a graph can form the boundary of a surface map if and only if it can be embedded in a surface of a given genus, with all its faces being single polygons.

This study introduces an innovative strategy for streamlining the communication burden of consensus-based stochastic optimization techniques. To achieve this objective, we integrate a versatile communication framework called Dynamic Neighborhoods into these methods. Our framework offers significant flexibility in arranging communication patterns, allowing for concurrent or sequential communication channels, as well as multi-way communication exchanges, all aimed at minimizing the overall communication overhead. To illustrate this concept, we develop a generalized version of Stochastic Gradient Descent with this framework, denoted as dynDG-SGD. Theoretical insights into asymptotic convergence rates for various optimization algorithms within the consensus framework have been established by Nesterov et al. Our analysis shows that a particular instance of dynDG-SGD can match these rates under certain conditions, thereby matching optimal performance. To validate our theoretical findings, we conducted an experiment that showed how reducing communication rounds by a factor of five using optimized communication schedules could maintain first-order accuracy of the results.

Transfer learning allows models to efficiently train in low-resource languages by leveraging a pre-trained model from a language family. This research explores the transfer capabilities between Romance languages by comparing three methods of extending a base model from French, Italian, and Spanish to Spanish, Russian and Ukrainian, and finally Ukrainian. Experimental findings reveal that direct extension from a language that's linguistically closer results in better performance, while extending from a pre-trained multilingual model yields comparable performance in terms of resource usage.

A crucial aspect of dark matter research involves identifying a specific signal, which can either be caused by electrons or by atomic nuclei. Researchers have developed techniques to differentiate between these two options in Liquid Argon detectors. This work presents an alternative approach to evaluating the effectiveness of distinguishing electron signals from nuclear ones in a Gas Time Projection Chamber. A simulation of a dark matter detector was conducted, and the results showed that by incorporating the impact of newly calculated observables, along with previously used methods, the ability to accurately differentiate between electron signals and nuclear ones was significantly improved, particularly for low energy releases below 1 keV. The use of advanced statistical analysis, including machine learning and multivariate analysis, yielded a 99% success rate in identifying nuclear recoil signals, a notable increase from the previously achieved 80% rate.

This research addresses the complexity of assessing driver behavior in areas such as fatigue and distraction by exploring how driver monitoring systems can be enhanced through external input. We propose a data-driven method that translates environmental conditions into a format usable by the driver. This approach involves creating a mapping between driver states and environmental features, followed by training a probabilistic model that predicts the likelihood of those features given the driver state and vehicle data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique using simulations and show that incorporating external input results in driver behavior detection on par with current methods. Furthermore, we highlight the potential benefits of this approach in improving communication between autonomous vehicles and humans.

This study introduces a comprehensive English Scene Text Dataset (ESTD), designed to enhance the evaluation of scene text recognition models. We expand existing datasets with a newly created component, the Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) dataset, to better reflect the diversity of real-world scene text and push models to more rigorous benchmarks. We exten existing datasets by grouping scene text texts according to their semantic categories and then supplement this with the OOV dataset, which features rare and unique text instances not previously seen by models. To assess the robustness of existing scene text recognition models, we extend them with the ESTD and evaluate their performance using both standard and OOV datasets. Furthermore, we present results demonstrating the significant impact of using distributionally grouped data, which significantly improves the accuracy of scene text recognition models.

In the laboratory setting, magnetic levitation creates a stable environment for objects in free fall. This technique is used to study the behavior of a liquid droplet when subjected to external forces. Our research builds upon previous studies that have shown how magnetic levitation can cause a slight shift in experiments due to the magnet's influence. To quantify this effect, we conducted experiments using a droplet of liquid helium and measured the initial distortion it undergoes under magnetic levitation. Our results show that the shape of the droplet changes in response to its height and the strength of the magnetic field, providing insight into the unique properties of superfluid helium droplets in magnetic levitation.

It is known that Hecke L-functions of primitive Sl2(Z) eigenforms display a certain level of randomness. This randomness is more pronounced than that of Spn(Z) eigenforms. This article seeks to systemize the randomness of Sl2(Z) L-functions, building on the work of a comprehensive conjecture proposed by the first author. This article aims to demonstrate that the distribution of central values for a family of primitive Hecke L-functions can be approximated by the distribution of a random signed sum of squares of Hecke eigenvalues. This random sum adheres to a probability measure known as the arcsine law. This article also aims to generalize the arcsine law to the Gaussian multiplicative chaos measure. This new, more rigorous approach will lead to precise Generalized Riemann Hypothesis analogues for Spn(Z) and Sl2(Z) L-functions.
